# V3·TA1 — Conditional types and infer

You have written conditional types before. `d15_conditional_types` gave you the
syntax and `d16_infer_patterns` gave you the keyword, and with those two you can
already write `ElementOf`, `ReturnType` and a dozen small utilities. That is the
level at which conditional types are pleasant.

This sector is about the level at which they are exact. The difference shows up
the first time you write a type test that quietly returns `never`, or an
`IsNever` that answers `never`, or a `ReturnType` that picks the wrong overload,
or a generic function whose return type the compiler refuses to accept as its
own body's type. None of those are syntax problems. They are all consequences of
three rules that the surface syntax hides: conditional types **distribute** over
unions when the checked type is naked, `infer` **collects candidates** and
combines them by variance, and a conditional type over an unresolved type
parameter is **deferred** rather than evaluated.

Get those three straight and the rest of the type-level toolkit — mapped types,
template literals, recursion — is mostly bookkeeping on top.

## Distribution, precisely

```ts
type Boxed<T> = T extends unknown ? { value: T } : never;
type R = Boxed<string | number>;
// { value: string } | { value: number }   — not { value: string | number }
```

The rule: when the type on the left of `extends` is a *naked* type parameter —
the parameter itself, not `T[]`, not `[T]`, not `Wrapper<T>` — the compiler
splits the union, evaluates the conditional once per member, and unions the
results. `Exclude`, `Extract` and `NonNullable` are nothing but this rule with
different branches.

Two consequences catch everyone once.

**The empty union.** `never` is the union with no members. Distributing over it
runs the conditional zero times, and the union of nothing is `never`:

```ts
type IsNeverWrong<T> = T extends never ? true : false;
type W = IsNeverWrong<never>;   // never, not true
```

**`any` takes both branches.** `any` is assignable to everything and everything
is assignable to it, so a distributive conditional over `any` produces the union
of the true and false branches:

```ts
type Test<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no";
type A = Test<any>;   // "yes" | "no"
```

The off switch for both is the tuple wrap, `[T] extends [U]`. It works because
`[T]` is not a naked type parameter, so the distribution rule simply does not
apply. `IsNever<T>` is `[T] extends [never] ? true : false` and there is no
other correct spelling.

## `infer`, and where the candidates come from

`infer X` declares a type variable inside an `extends` pattern and binds it to
whatever the matcher found. What is worth internalising is that the same `X` can
appear in several positions, and that the compiler then has several candidates
to reconcile:

```ts
type Cov<T> = T extends { a: infer U; b: infer U } ? U : never;
type Con<F> = F extends (a: infer U, b: infer U) => unknown ? U : never;

type C1 = Cov<{ a: string; b: number }>;              // string | number
type C2 = Con<(a: { x: 1 }, b: { y: 2 }) => void>;    // { x: 1 } & { y: 2 }
```

Covariant positions (property types, return types, array elements) union their
candidates. Contravariant positions (function parameters) intersect them. That
is not an arbitrary choice: a value *read* from either of two places could be
either, while a function *given* to both places has to handle both. The whole
`UnionToIntersection` trick in ex4 is this rule, deliberately provoked.

Two more `infer` facts you will use this sector:

- `infer X extends string` (TypeScript 4.8) constrains the inference site, so a
  pattern can fail to match instead of binding something useless.
- An `infer` that matches nothing falls back to `unknown`, which is why
  `FirstArg<() => void>` is `unknown` rather than an error.

## Deferred conditionals

Inside a generic function, a conditional type over the function's own type
parameter cannot be evaluated — the parameter is not known yet — so it stays
*deferred*. A deferred conditional is assignable to almost nothing, including
the thing you just computed:

```ts
type Wrapped<T> = T extends string ? string[] : T[];

function wrap<T>(value: T): Wrapped<T> {
  return [value];   // Type 'T[]' is not assignable to type 'Wrapped<T>'.
}
```

The compiler is right and there is no clever type that fixes it. The accepted
answer is an overload or an internal implementation signature and one honest
cast at the boundary, which is exactly what `lib.dom.d.ts` and every serious
library do. Recognising this error saves you an afternoon.

## `Equal`, and why the obvious version is wrong

Every exercise in this sector is checked with the same pair:

```ts
type Equal<A, B> =
  (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;
```

That looks like a joke and is not. It compares two *deferred* conditional types
by identity, which is the only way to get the checker to answer "are these the
same type" rather than "is each assignable to the other". The naive version:

```ts
type Naive<A, B> = A extends B ? (B extends A ? true : false) : false;
```

reports `true` for `{ a?: string }` versus `{ a: string | undefined }`, which
are genuinely different types, and produces `boolean` when either side is `any`.
You will implement the real one in ex8.

## ex1 — the only correct way to ask "is this never?"

`IsNever<T>` plus a `NeverKeys<T>` that lists the keys whose value type is
`never`. Watch what an *optional* `never` property does.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex1
```

## ex2 — detecting `any` and `unknown`

`IsAny<T>` and `IsUnknown<T>`, where the second one has to rule out the first.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex2
```

## ex3 — distribution, used on purpose

`Exclusive<A, B>` (symmetric difference) and `SharedWith<A, B>` (`Extract` by
hand), including the `never` edge.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex3
```

## ex4 — union to intersection

The one type every advanced library contains exactly once.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex4
```

## ex5 — inferring through a constructor

`Constructed<C>` and `CtorArgs<C>`, matching abstract classes and preserving
parameter labels.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex5
```

## ex6 — two candidates, one `infer`

Prove the union/intersection rule to yourself by writing both halves.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex6
```

## ex7 — unwrap every thenable

`Settled<T>`: recursive unwrapping through the structural `then` pattern, the
way the standard library's `Awaited` does it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex7
```

## ex8 — the equality type itself

Write `Equal`, `NotEqual` and `Expect`, and make them survive `any` and
optionality.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex8
```

## Challenge — `UnionToTuple`

Turn a union into a tuple, in declaration order, using `UnionToIntersection`,
last-overload inference and an accumulator recursion.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer challenge
```

## Review — an event bus that types its own payloads

`EventOf<K>`, `PayloadOf<K>` and a `dispatch` that ties a handler to the payload
of the event it was given.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer review1
```

# Reading - typescript/v3ta01_conditional_types_infer

Notes on the three rules, then one paragraph per mission on what it was really
testing.

## Notes

**Distribution is a property of the checked type, not of the conditional.** The
compiler asks one question: is the type on the left of `extends` a naked type
parameter? If yes, split the union and recombine the results. If no — because
you wrote `[T]`, or `T[]`, or `Foo<T>`, or a concrete type — evaluate once. This
is why the tuple wrap works, why `Exclude` distributes and `IsNever` must not,
and why a conditional written inside another type alias sometimes stops
distributing when you refactor it. The refactor changed the nakedness.

**`never` is the empty union and behaves like one everywhere.** Distributing
over it produces `never`. A union containing `never` drops it: `string | never`
is `string`. A mapped type whose value is `never` still has the key; an indexed
access `{ ... }[keyof T]` that unions `never`s away is the standard key-filter
idiom because of that. And `never` is assignable to everything, which is why an
unreachable branch typed `never` never complains.

**`any` short-circuits every check.** In a distributive conditional it takes
both branches and yields the union of them. In an assignability test it is true
in both directions. `IsAny<T> = 0 extends 1 & T ? true : false` works because
`1 & any` collapses back to `any` while `1 & T` is `1` (or `never`) for
everything else — an intersection that widens is the fingerprint of `any`.

**Inference candidates combine by variance.** Multiple `infer X` sites in
covariant position produce a union; in contravariant position, an intersection.
This is the mechanism, not a special case: it is the same variance that decides
whether `(x: Animal) => void` is assignable to `(x: Dog) => void`. It also
explains a fact that surprises people: `ReturnType` of an overloaded function is
the return type of the *last* overload, because inference against an overloaded
signature tries the overloads in order from the bottom.

**Deferred conditionals are the compiler being honest.** `Wrapped<T>` where `T`
is unresolved is a type the checker cannot reduce, and it will not pretend
otherwise. Practically: put the conditional in the public signature, give the
implementation a looser internal signature, and cast once where you can see the
invariant. A cast you can point at beats a type that lies everywhere.

**Type equality is not mutual assignability.** `{ a?: string }` and
`{ a: string | undefined }` are mutually assignable and are not the same type;
`any` is mutually assignable with everything. The `Equal` type compares two
generic function types whose bodies are deferred conditionals, and the checker
compares those by structural identity of the deferred type. It is a
well-documented exploitation of internal behaviour, it has been stable for
years, and every type-testing library uses it.

## ex1 — IsNever

The exercise is a trap with a one-line escape. If you wrote
`T extends never ? true : false` and got `never`, you learned the empty-union
rule the way that sticks. `NeverKeys` then puts the predicate to work, and slips
in a second lesson: `also?: never` declares the property as `never | undefined`,
which is just `undefined`, so it is not a never-key at all. Optional and `never`
do not compose the way the syntax suggests.

## ex2 — IsAny and IsUnknown

`IsAny` is a puzzle with one known answer, and it is worth being able to
reconstruct rather than memorise: find a proposition false for every real type
and true for `any`. `IsUnknown` is the ordering lesson — `[unknown] extends [T]`
is true for both `unknown` and `any`, so the `any` test has to come first. Any
predicate you build over these two inherits that ordering requirement.

## ex3 — Exclusive and SharedWith

Distribution used as a tool. The interesting assertion is
`Exclusive<never, "a">` being `"a"`: the first difference distributes over zero
members and contributes `never`, the second contributes `"a"`, and `never | "a"`
is `"a"`. If you reached for a tuple wrap here you would have broken it — the
skill is knowing which of your conditionals wants distribution on and which
wants it off.

## ex4 — UnionToIntersection

Two conditionals stacked: one distributive, to build a union of one-parameter
functions; one with `infer` in the parameter slot, to collapse that union into
an intersection. `UnionToIntersection<string | number>` being `never` is not a
failure — `string & number` has no inhabitants and the checker reduces it.

## ex5 — constructor inference

`abstract new (...)` exists because `InstanceType` could not describe abstract
classes before TypeScript 4.2, and mixin factories kept hitting it. The labelled
tuple in the expected output is the second point: `(...args: infer A)` binds the
whole parameter tuple, and since TypeScript 4.0 that tuple keeps its labels, so
`CtorArgs<typeof Repo>` is `[url: string, retries: number]` and not just
`[string, number]`. Labels are part of type identity for `Equal`.

## ex6 — candidate combination

The two halves of the same rule, side by side, so that ex4 stops being a magic
incantation. If you can explain why the contravariant case *must* intersect —
a function passed to both call sites has to accept both arguments — you can
derive `UnionToIntersection` from scratch instead of copying it.

## ex7 — Settled

Matching `{ then(onfulfilled: (value: infer V) => unknown, ...rest: never[]): unknown }`
rather than `Promise<infer V>` is what makes this work on any thenable,
including the ones libraries hand you. The `null | undefined` guard at the front
is not decoration: without it the distribution over a union containing `null`
would try to match `then` on `null` and produce a subtly wrong result. The
standard library's `Awaited` has the same guard for the same reason.

## ex8 — Equal

Writing the equality type is the point at which you stop trusting `extends` as
an equality test. Keep the `NotEqual` you wrote — a test suite that only asserts
positives will happily pass against a type that returns `any` everywhere.

## challenge — UnionToTuple

Three ideas at once: `UnionToIntersection` to build an intersection of function
types, inference against that intersection to pull out the *last* signature, and
a tail-recursive accumulator that removes the extracted member and goes round
again. It also has an honest caveat: union member order is an implementation
detail of the checker, not a language guarantee. It is stable enough that
libraries depend on it, and you should know that you are depending on it.

## review1 — the event bus

`Extract<AppEvent, { type: K }>` is `SharedWith` from ex3 wearing work clothes,
and because it distributes, `PayloadOf<"user:created" | "ping">` is the union of
both payloads rather than an error. The `dispatch` implementation needs one cast
— the deferred-conditional problem from the briefing, in its most common
real-world disguise.

# V3·TA1 — Conditional types and infer (archive)

The deep version: the mechanism, worked examples, the mistakes that cost hours,
the interview answer, and a question bank.

## 1. The distribution rule in full

A conditional type `T extends U ? X : Y` is *distributive* when `T` is a naked
type parameter. Naked means the type parameter appears alone as the checked
type. All of these are naked:

```ts
type A<T> = T extends string ? 1 : 0;
type B<T> = T extends string ? { v: T } : never;   // branches don't matter
```

None of these are:

```ts
type C<T> = [T] extends [string] ? 1 : 0;
type D<T> = T[] extends string[] ? 1 : 0;
type E<T> = Wrapper<T> extends string ? 1 : 0;
type F<T> = (T & {}) extends string ? 1 : 0;
```

When it distributes, the compiler evaluates the conditional once per union
member and unions the results. Three special cases:

```ts
type Test<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no";

type R1 = Test<"a" | 1>;    // "yes" | "no"
type R2 = Test<never>;      // never       — zero members, union of nothing
type R3 = Test<any>;        // "yes" | "no" — any takes both branches
```

`boolean` is worth knowing about too: it is `true | false` internally, so it
distributes into two members. `Test<boolean>` runs twice.

### Turning it off

```ts
type IsNever<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false;
type IsBoolean<T> = [T] extends [boolean] ? true : false;   // true for boolean, false for true
```

Wrap *both* sides. `[T] extends never` is not the same check and will mislead
you.

## 2. `infer` positions worth knowing

```ts
type El<T>       = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never;
type Ret<F>      = F extends (...args: never[]) => infer R ? R : never;
type Args<F>     = F extends (...args: infer A) => unknown ? A : never;
type First<F>    = F extends (first: infer P, ...rest: never[]) => unknown ? P : never;
type Inst<C>     = C extends abstract new (...args: never[]) => infer R ? R : never;
type Head<T>     = T extends readonly [infer H, ...unknown[]] ? H : never;
type Prop<T>     = T extends { value: infer V } ? V : never;
type Num<S>      = S extends `${infer N extends number}` ? N : never;
```

Rules that apply to all of them:

- `infer` is legal **only** inside the `extends` clause of a conditional type,
  and the variable is in scope **only** in the true branch.
- An `infer` with no candidate resolves to `unknown`.
- `infer X extends C` (4.8) both constrains the match and, for the numeric and
  boolean cases over template literals, converts the matched string literal into
  the corresponding literal type.
- Multiple candidates: union in covariant position, intersection in
  contravariant position.

### The overload rule

```ts
declare function parse(input: string): number;
declare function parse(input: string[]): number[];

type R = ReturnType<typeof parse>;   // number[]
```

Inference against an overloaded function type uses the *last* overload. This is
a documented consequence of how the checker picks a signature to match against,
and it is the reason `Parameters<typeof someOverloadedThing>` so often looks
wrong. If you need a specific overload, extract it with an explicit pattern or
restructure the declaration.

## 3. Deferred conditional types

```ts
type Wrapped<T> = T extends string ? string[] : T[];

function wrap<T>(value: T): Wrapped<T> {
  return [value];
  // error TS2322: Type 'T[]' is not assignable to type 'Wrapped<T>'.
}
```

`Wrapped<T>` cannot be reduced while `T` is unresolved, so it is an opaque type
that only equals itself. Nothing you write in the body will satisfy it. The
three real options:

```ts
// 1. Overloads with a permissive implementation signature.
function wrap(value: string): string[];
function wrap<T>(value: T): T[];
function wrap(value: unknown): unknown[] { return [value]; }

// 2. Public conditional signature, internal cast.
function wrap2<T>(value: T): Wrapped<T> {
  return [value] as Wrapped<T>;
}

// 3. Don't use a conditional return type. Often the right answer.
```

Prefer 1 when callers pass literals, 2 when the invariant is genuinely simple,
and 3 more often than you would like to admit.

## 4. The equality type

```ts
type Equal<A, B> =
  (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
```

Why this and not mutual assignability:

| pair | mutually assignable | `Equal` |
|---|---|---|
| `any` / `string` | yes | `false` |
| `{ a?: string }` / `{ a: string \| undefined }` | yes | `false` |
| `[a: string]` / `[string]` | yes | `false` |
| `1 \| 2` / `2 \| 1` | yes | `true` |

The last row matters: `Equal` is not sensitive to union member order, which is
what you want in a test. The third row matters too — tuple labels are part of
identity, so an assertion about `Parameters<...>` has to spell the labels.

## 5. Common mistakes

**Writing `T extends never`.** Always `never`. Use the tuple wrap.

**Assuming a helper type still distributes.** Wrapping a distributive
conditional in another alias keeps distribution only if the inner checked type
is still the naked parameter of the *inner* alias. Refactoring
`T extends U ? ... : ...` into `Helper<T>` where `Helper` immediately wraps in a
tuple silently changes behaviour.

**Testing types with only positive assertions.** A type that resolves to `any`
passes every `extends`-based check. Assert a `false` somewhere.

**Reaching for `infer` where an index would do.** `T["payload"]` beats
`T extends { payload: infer P } ? P : never` in both readability and compile
time. Use `infer` when the thing you want is *inside* a structure that indexed
access cannot reach — a parameter list, a return type, a template literal
segment.

**Forgetting the `null | undefined` guard in recursive unwrappers.** Any
recursive conditional that distributes should decide explicitly what it does
with nullish members before it starts pattern matching.

**Deep nesting instead of naming.** A five-level conditional is unreadable and
slow to check. Name the intermediate steps; the compiler caches aliases and your
reviewer thanks you.

## 6. The interview answer

If someone asks "what is a conditional type", the mediocre answer is "a ternary
for types". The good answer is three sentences:

> A conditional type is a type-level `if` that the checker evaluates by
> assignability. When its checked type is a bare type parameter it distributes
> over unions, which is how `Exclude` and `Extract` work and why `IsNever` has
> to disable distribution with a tuple wrap. `infer` declares a variable inside
> the pattern, and when the same variable appears in several positions the
> candidates are unioned in covariant positions and intersected in contravariant
> ones — which is exactly what `UnionToIntersection` exploits.

Then, if they push: mention deferred conditionals inside generic functions, and
that the standard fix is an internal implementation signature. That answer
signals you have shipped this stuff rather than read about it.

## 7. Check yourself

1. What does `T extends never ? true : false` evaluate to for `T = never`, and
   why?
2. Which of `[T] extends [U]`, `T[] extends U[]`, `T extends U` distribute?
3. What is `Exclude<never, string>`? What is `Exclude<string, never>`?
4. Why is `UnionToIntersection<string | number>` equal to `never`?
5. Write `IsAny<T>` and explain the intersection trick in one sentence.
6. Where is an `infer` variable in scope, and what does an unmatched `infer`
   resolve to?
7. Two `infer U` sites in property positions produce what? Two in parameter
   positions?
8. What is `ReturnType` of a function with three overloads, and why?
9. Give an example of two types that are mutually assignable but not `Equal`.
10. Why does the compiler reject `return [value];` in a function returning
    `Wrapped<T>`, and what are your three options?
11. What does `infer N extends number` add over plain `infer N` in a template
    literal pattern?
12. Why does `{ a?: never }` not count as a key with value type `never`?
13. What happens when you distribute a conditional over `boolean`?
14. Why is `abstract new (...)` the better pattern for a constructor-matching
    conditional type?

# Reading - typescript/v3ta01_conditional_types_infer (long form)

## Where conditional types came from

Conditional types landed in TypeScript 2.8, in February 2018, and the release
note gave them a modest billing: a way to express non-uniform type mappings.
What actually shipped was a small functional language embedded in the type
system, and the design decisions taken that day are the ones you are still
living with.

The central decision was distribution. Anders Hejlsberg's design notes for the
feature argue that if you write `Exclude<T, U>` you almost always mean "for each
member of T, keep it unless it is in U", so making the naked-type-parameter case
distribute automatically turns a whole family of utilities into one-liners. The
alternative — an explicit `distribute T over ...` operator — would have been
more honest and much more verbose. The compromise was to make distribution the
default for the one syntactic shape where it is usually wanted, and to give you
an off switch that is not a keyword but an idiom: wrap in a tuple.

That is why the off switch looks like a hack. It is not; it is a direct
consequence of the rule being purely syntactic. The checker literally asks
whether the checked type node resolves to a type parameter with nothing around
it. `[T]` puts something around it, and the question answers itself.

`infer` shipped in the same release. It is the pattern-matching half, and it
reuses machinery that already existed: the inference engine that resolves
generic call arguments. When you write `F extends (...args: infer A) => unknown`,
the checker runs the same candidate-collection algorithm it runs when it infers
`T` for `identity(someValue)`. That reuse is why the variance rules match — you
are not learning a new rule for `infer`, you are seeing the ordinary inference
rule from a new angle.

Later releases filled in the gaps. TypeScript 4.0 gave tuples labels and
variadic positions, so `infer` against parameter lists became precise. 4.1 added
template literal types and, importantly, tail-recursion-friendly evaluation of
conditional types, which is what makes recursive string parsers viable at all.
4.2 added `abstract new` so that construct-signature patterns could match
abstract classes. 4.7 added variance annotations (`in`, `out`) on type
parameters. 4.8 added `infer X extends C`, which does two jobs: it filters the
match, and for numeric and boolean constraints against template literal
segments, it produces a literal type of the constrained kind rather than a
string.

## How the checker actually evaluates one

Roughly, when the checker meets `T extends U ? X : Y`:

1. It resolves the checked type. If that resolution is still an unresolved type
   parameter or contains one in a way that blocks a decision, the whole
   conditional becomes a **deferred conditional type** — an object in the
   checker's type table that remembers the four components and is compared to
   other types by identity, not by content.
2. If the checked type resolved to a union and the *syntactic* checked type was
   a naked type parameter, it maps the conditional over the members and unions
   the results. The mapping is lazy; the results are cached per instantiation.
3. Otherwise it performs an assignability check of the resolved checked type
   against the extends type, running inference first if the pattern contains
   `infer` sites, collecting candidates per site.
4. Candidates are combined: union for covariant sites, intersection for
   contravariant ones. Sites with no candidate become `unknown` — or, when an
   `extends` constraint is present, the constraint.
5. The winning branch is instantiated with the `infer` bindings in scope.

Two practical facts fall out of this. First, the identity comparison in step 1
is exactly what the `Equal` type exploits: two deferred conditionals compare
equal only if their components are identical, so wrapping `A` and `B` in
structurally identical deferred conditionals turns "are these the same type" into
a question the checker can answer precisely. Second, the caching in step 2 is
per instantiation, which means a distributive conditional over a large union is
work proportional to the union's size — and if the branches are themselves
conditionals over the same union, that work multiplies.

## Performance, honestly

Conditional types are not free. The costs that actually show up in real
codebases, in the order they usually bite:

- **Large distributive unions.** A conditional distributing over a 500-member
  union does 500 instantiations, and any nested conditional inside it multiplies.
  A template literal type over a cross-product of two such unions is how teams
  discover the checker's 100,000-member union limit.
- **Deeply nested conditionals.** Each level is another instantiation to cache
  and another node in error messages. Five levels turns a type error into an
  unreadable wall.
- **Recursion without an accumulator.** Non-tail-recursive conditional types hit
  the instantiation depth limit and produce error TS2589, "Type instantiation is
  excessively deep and possibly infinite". The next sector on recursion covers
  the rewrite.
- **Re-instantiation at every call site.** A generic function whose return type
  is a complex conditional re-evaluates it for every distinct argument type in
  your program. This is the difference between a build that takes 20 seconds and
  one that takes three minutes.

`tsc --extendedDiagnostics` gives you check time and instantiation counts;
`--generateTrace out/` gives you a Chrome-trace file you can open in
`chrome://tracing` and read as a flame graph of type checking. If a type is slow,
measure it before you rewrite it — the culprit is usually one alias, not the
whole file.

## When not to reach for a conditional type

The honest list is longer than the tutorials suggest.

**When an indexed access will do.** `T["payload"]`, `T[keyof T]`, and
`Parameters<F>[0]` are cheaper to check and easier to read than the equivalent
conditional pattern.

**When an overload will do.** If you have three concrete input shapes and three
concrete output shapes, three overloads are clearer to your callers, produce
better error messages, and do not create a deferred type that fights your
implementation.

**When the conditional is in a public API's return type.** Every caller now has
a type they cannot inspect in a hover and cannot easily narrow. Sometimes it is
worth it — `Awaited<T>` earns it — but the bar should be high.

**When you are encoding business logic.** A type that computes which permissions
a role has is a joy to write and a liability to maintain: it is invisible to
your test suite, cannot be logged, and fails at compile time with a message that
mentions none of the domain. Values can do that job, and `satisfies` will keep
them honest.

**When the alternative is a discriminated union.** Most of the time you do not
need a type-level function; you need a better data model. A four-variant union
with an exhaustive switch is more readable than a conditional type that computes
the same four cases, and it exists at runtime where you can debug it.

The rule of thumb worth carrying out of this sector: conditional types are for
describing relationships between types that already exist in your program. When
you find yourself using them to *invent* types your program does not otherwise
have, stop and check whether a value would do.

## Debugging a conditional type

There is no debugger for the type system, so you need a method. The one that
works:

1. **Make the failure concrete.** Replace the generic call site with a hard-coded
   instantiation — `type Probe = MyType<"a" | "b">` — and hover it. A type that
   is wrong at a concrete instantiation is much easier to reason about than one
   that is wrong somewhere inside a generic function.
2. **Bisect the alias.** Split the conditional into named steps, one alias per
   level, and hover each. Nine times out of ten one step produced `never` or
   `unknown` several levels before the symptom.
3. **Check for the three usual suspects at every `never`.** Empty-union
   distribution, an `infer` that matched nothing and fell back, or a pattern that
   silently failed to match and took the false branch.
4. **Assert a negative.** Add `Expect<Equal<Something, false>>` alongside your
   positive assertions. A type that has quietly become `any` passes every
   positive test you can write.
5. **Only then read the error message.** Conditional-type errors name the
   deferred type rather than its expansion, so they tell you where the checker
   gave up, not where you went wrong. The hover is the better instrument.

That method transfers to every remaining sector in this volume: mapped types,
template literals and recursive types all fail in the same silent way, and all
of them respond to the same bisect-and-hover discipline.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## ex1 - the only correct way to ask "is this never?"

`IsNever<T>` is `true` when `T` is exactly `never`, and `false` for everything
else. The obvious spelling, `T extends never ? true : false`, is wrong, and the
gate proves it.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement two types:

```ts
export type IsNever<T> = /* ... */;
export type NeverKeys<T> = /* ... */;   // the keys of T whose value type is never
```

The gate defines the usual pair:

```ts
type Equal<A, B> =
  (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;
```

and asserts:

```ts
type _1 = Expect<Equal<IsNever<never>, true>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<IsNever<string>, false>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<IsNever<never | string>, false>>;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<IsNever<any>, false>>;
type _5 = Expect<Equal<NeverKeys<{ ok: string; dead: never; also?: never }>, "dead">>;
```

That last line is not a typo. `also?: never` has the declared type
`never | undefined`, which collapses to `undefined` before your type ever sees
it - so it is not a `never` key. Read the assertion, then work out why.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`T extends never ? true : false` fails on `IsNever<never>` for a reason that
has nothing to do with `never` being empty. A conditional type whose checked
type is a *naked* type parameter distributes over a union, and `never` is the
empty union. Distributing over no members means there is nothing to evaluate,
so the result is `never` - not `true`, not `false`.

## Hint 2

Distribution is switched off by wrapping both sides in a one-element tuple.
This is exactly how `NonNullable` used to be written, and how the standard
library still writes the trick when it needs it:

```ts
type IsBoolean<T> = [T] extends [boolean] ? true : false;
```

The tuple is not doing anything clever. It just means the checked type is no
longer a bare `T`, so the distribution rule does not apply.

## Hint 3

`IsNever` is one line with the tuple wrap. `NeverKeys` is a mapped type whose
value is the key itself when the property is `never` and `never` otherwise,
immediately indexed by `keyof T` to collapse it to a union - the standard
"filter keys" shape:

```ts
type Filtered<T> = { [K in keyof T]: /* K or never */ }[keyof T];
```

Left to you: whether that mapped type needs `-?`. Try it both ways and use the
`also?: never` assertion to decide which answer the compiler actually gives.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the error rather than the theory. Write the naive version, then ask
the compiler what it produced:

```ts
type Naive<T> = T extends never ? true : false;
type Probe = Naive<never>;
//   ^? hover it
```

The hover says `never`, not `false`. Any time a conditional type evaluates to
`never` when you expected a boolean, you are looking at empty-union
distribution, not a logic bug.

## Hint 2

There are only three checked-type shapes worth memorising:

| you write | distributes? |
|---|---|
| `T extends U ? A : B` | yes, when `T` is a bare type parameter |
| `[T] extends [U] ? A : B` | no |
| `SomeAlias<T> extends U ? A : B` | no - the alias is not naked |

Every "why is my conditional type `never`" question resolves to the first row.

## Hint 3

For `NeverKeys`, build it in two steps and hover after each. First the mapped
type alone, which gives you an object whose values are keys-or-`never`; then
index it with `[keyof T]`, which unions the values and drops the `never`s for
free - a union with `never` in it is just the union without it.

Left to you: whether `IsNever<T[K]> extends true ? K : never` or the direct
`[T[K]] extends [never] ? K : never` reads better. Both compile; one of them
reuses the type you just wrote.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Find a proposition that is false for every type in the language and true for
`any`. Intersection is the lever: `1 & T` is `1` for most `T`, but `1 & any` is
`any` - and `0 extends any` is true.

## Hint 2

The same shape appears in the standard library's `NonNullable` neighbourhood
and in every type-testing library:

```ts
type IsNumberOrAny<T> = 1 extends 2 & T ? "any" : T extends number ? "number" : "no";
```

Read the middle term as "an intersection that only widens back to `any` when
`T` was `any`".

## Hint 3

`IsUnknown` is layered on top of `IsAny`. `unknown` is the type everything is
assignable to, so `[unknown] extends [T]` is true for `unknown` - and also for
`any`, because `any` swallows every check. Rule out `any` first, then ask
whether `T` is a supertype of `unknown`.

Left to you: whether `never` needs a case of its own. Reason about
`[unknown] extends [never]` before you add one, then let the gate confirm it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build the truth table before you write a line. For each candidate `T`, which of
these is true?

| T | `T extends string` | `[unknown] extends [T]` | `0 extends 1 & T` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `any` | both branches | true | true |
| `unknown` | false | true | false |
| `never` | neither (distributes to `never`) | false | false |

Only the last column separates `any` from everything else, which is why it is
the primitive you build on.

## Hint 2

`any` in a distributive conditional produces the *union of both branches*, not
one of them:

```ts
type Weird<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no";
type R = Weird<any>;   // "yes" | "no"
```

That is worth knowing on its own: if a type test returns `boolean` where you
expected `true` or `false`, an `any` reached it.

## Hint 3

Write `IsUnknown` as a two-level nest: reject `any` first, then ask whether
`unknown` is assignable to `T`. The second question is the definition of
"`T` is `unknown` or wider", and nothing in the language is wider.

Left to you: whether that second check needs the tuple wrap at all. Work out
which side of `unknown extends T` is the naked type parameter before you
decide - the distribution rule only ever looks at the checked type, the one on
the left.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A symmetric difference is "in A and not in B, or in B and not in A". Written
in set notation it is two set-differences unioned, and TypeScript already ships
the set-difference operator under a different name.

## Hint 2

`Extract` and `Exclude` are the same conditional type with the branches
swapped:

```ts
type Exclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;
type Extract<T, U> = T extends U ? T : never;
```

Both work because `T` is naked: the conditional runs once per union member, and
the members that map to `never` vanish from the resulting union.

## Hint 3

`SharedWith` is one line and is `Extract` spelled out. `Exclusive` is a union
of two set-differences with the arguments swapped the second time.

Left to you: whether to define the difference helper yourself or lean on the
built-in `Exclude`. The `never` assertion behaves identically either way - work
out why before you assume it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Trace `Exclusive<1 | 2 | 3, 2 | 3 | 4>` by hand as the compiler would. For the
first half the checked type has three members, so the conditional runs three
times: `1`, then `2`, then `3`, each against the whole of `2 | 3 | 4`. Write the
three results down. The union of them is half your answer.

## Hint 2

The dangerous half is the empty case. `Exclusive<never, "a">` runs the first
difference over zero members, which yields `never` - correct, nothing in the
empty set is exclusive to it - and the second over `"a"`, which yields `"a"`.
The union `never | "a"` is `"a"`.

Contrast that with a version that tried to be clever and lost distribution:

```ts
type Bad<A, B> = [A] extends [B] ? never : A | B;   // wrong answers everywhere
```

## Hint 3

Two named helpers or two inline conditionals, then a union. The whole solution
is four lines including the exports.

Left to you: whether `SharedWith<A, B>` should also distribute over `B`. It does
not need to, and knowing why - only the checked type distributes - is the point
of the exercise.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - union to intersection

This is the type that every advanced TypeScript library contains exactly once,
and the reason `infer` in a parameter position is worth understanding.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export type UnionToIntersection<U> = /* ... */;
```

Expected:

```ts
type _1 = Expect<Equal<UnionToIntersection<{ a: 1 } | { b: 2 }>, { a: 1 } & { b: 2 }>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<UnionToIntersection<string | number>, never>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<UnionToIntersection<{ a: 1 }>, { a: 1 }>>;
```

The second assertion is not a bug in your solution. `string & number` is a type
with no inhabitants and the compiler reduces it to `never`; a union of
primitives genuinely has no intersection.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The trick has two halves. First turn the union `A | B` into a union of
functions `((x: A) => void) | ((x: B) => void)`. Then infer a single parameter
type out of that union. The second step is where the intersection appears.

## Hint 2

Function parameters are contravariant, so something that has to satisfy both
`(x: A) => void` and `(x: B) => void` must accept `A & B`. The compiler collects
one inference candidate per union member and, in a contravariant position,
intersects them instead of unioning them:

```ts
type Arg<F> = F extends (x: infer P) => void ? P : never;
type R = Arg<((x: string) => void) | ((x: number) => void)>;   // string & number
```

## Hint 3

Build the function union with a distributive conditional -
`U extends unknown ? (probe: U) => void : never` - then feed the whole thing to
a second conditional with `infer` in the parameter slot.

Left to you: the checked type of that first conditional. Something has to be
naked for it to distribute, and a distributive conditional whose branches ignore
the check is a perfectly normal way to write "map over this union".
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it from assignability instead of from types-as-code. Ask: which
function can I safely use where a `(x: { a: 1 }) => void` *or* a
`(x: { b: 2 }) => void` is expected, without knowing which? Only one that
accepts both shapes. Write that answer down; it is the type you are trying to
make the compiler compute.

## Hint 2

Two inference sites, same variable, different variance:

```ts
type Cov<T> = T extends { a: infer U; b: infer U } ? U : never;
type Con<F> = F extends (a: infer U, b: infer U) => void ? U : never;
```

`Cov<{ a: string; b: number }>` is `string | number`. `Con` on the analogous
function is `string & number`. Nothing about `infer` changed - only where it
appeared.

## Hint 3

Two nested conditionals, roughly:

```ts
type UnionToIntersection<U> =
  (/* build a union of one-parameter functions from U */) extends
    (probe: infer I) => void ? I : never;
```

Left to you: whether the inner conditional's false branch should be `never` or
something else. It is unreachable for every input the gate supplies, which is
its own small lesson about how much of a type's text is load-bearing.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The type-level spelling of "a thing you can call with `new`" is
`new (...args: never[]) => unknown`. An abstract class is not that - you cannot
`new` it. There is a separate modifier for the pattern that also matches
abstract constructors.

## Hint 2

`abstract new (...) => ...` is a legal type, added in TypeScript 4.2 precisely
so that mixins and `InstanceType`-shaped helpers could accept abstract classes:

```ts
type AnyCtor = abstract new (...args: never[]) => object;
declare function register<C extends AnyCtor>(ctor: C): void;
```

Every concrete constructor is assignable to an abstract one, so using
`abstract new` in the pattern costs nothing and matches strictly more types.

## Hint 3

Both types are one conditional each. For the arguments, `infer` the rest
parameter as a whole: `(...args: infer A)` binds `A` to the entire parameter
tuple, labels included.

Left to you: `never[]` or `any[]` for the throwaway args in `Constructed`. Both
pass this gate; only one of them keeps working when a constructor parameter is
itself generic, and the way to find out is to try one.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the failing version first and read the result. With a plain
`new (...args: never[]) => infer R` pattern, `Constructed<typeof Repo>` comes
out as `never` - and there is no error anywhere, because the conditional simply
took the false branch. Type-level bugs are silent; the only signal is the
assertion that stops matching.

## Hint 2

`typeof Repo` for an abstract class is not a constructor type in the usual
sense. Hover it: you get an object with the static side and an *abstract*
construct signature. The standard library hit the same wall - compare how
`InstanceType` and `ConstructorParameters` are declared in `lib.es5.d.ts` today
with how they were declared before TypeScript 4.2.

## Hint 3

Two conditionals, four lines. The parameter tuple falls out of a rest-parameter
`infer`; the instance type falls out of the return position of the construct
signature.

Left to you: whether `CtorArgs` should use `abstract new` as well. The gate only
asks about `Repo`, but decide the general rule rather than the one that happens
to pass.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## ex6 - two candidates, one `infer`

An `infer` variable that appears in more than one position collects more than
one candidate, and what the compiler does with them depends entirely on whether
those positions are covariant or contravariant. This is the mechanism behind
ex4.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export type CovariantCandidates<T> = /* U inferred from two property positions */;
export type ContravariantCandidates<F> = /* P inferred from two parameter positions */;
```

Expected:

```ts
type _1 = Expect<Equal<
  CovariantCandidates<{ first: string; second: number }>,
  string | number
>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<
  ContravariantCandidates<(first: { a: 1 }, second: { b: 2 }) => void>,
  { a: 1 } & { b: 2 }
>>;
```

Same keyword, same variable name used twice, opposite combining rule. Write
both, then say out loud why the difference is the only sound choice.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both types are a single conditional. The only design decision is the *pattern*
on the right of `extends`: an object type with two properties in the first case,
a two-parameter function type in the second. Use the same `infer` name in both
slots of each pattern.

## Hint 2

The shape you are aiming for, on a smaller example:

```ts
type SameTwice<T> = T extends { left: infer U; right: infer U } ? U : never;
type A = SameTwice<{ left: 1; right: 2 }>;   // 1 | 2
```

Move the two slots into parameter positions of a function type and the result
flips to an intersection.

## Hint 3

`CovariantCandidates<T>` matches `{ first: infer U; second: infer U }`;
`ContravariantCandidates<F>` matches `(first: infer P, second: infer P) => unknown`.

Left to you: `=> unknown` or `=> any` as the return type in that pattern. Both
match here. Pick the one you can defend to a reviewer.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Reason about it as a safety question, not a syntax question.

- A value read out of either of two covariant positions could have come from
  either one, so the only sound description is "one or the other": a union.
- A function handed to both contravariant positions must survive both calls, so
  the only sound description is "both at once": an intersection.

If the compiler chose the other way round in either case it would be unsound.

## Hint 2

The variance rule is not special to `infer`. It is the same rule that governs
assignability of function types, and you can watch it in ordinary code:

```ts
declare let strict: (x: { a: 1 } & { b: 2 }) => void;
declare let loose: (x: { a: 1 }) => void;
strict = loose;   // allowed: loose needs less than strict promises to supply
```

Inference is that rule run backwards.

## Hint 3

Write the covariant one first and confirm the union in a hover. Then copy it,
turn the object pattern into a function pattern, and confirm the intersection.

Left to you: whether to name the two `infer` variables the same in both types.
They are independent scopes, so it does not matter for correctness - but naming
them identically makes the contrast readable at a glance.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - unwrap every thenable, all the way down

`Awaited<T>` is in the standard library, but writing it teaches you three things
at once: structural matching, recursion in a conditional type, and why the
nullish guard comes first.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export type Settled<T> = /* ... */;
```

It must unwrap any object with a thenable `then` method - not only `Promise` -
and repeat until there is nothing left to unwrap.

Expected:

```ts
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Settled<Promise<Promise<string>>>, string>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Settled<number>, number>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<Settled<Promise<string> | number>, string | number>>;
type _4 = Expect<Equal<Settled<null>, null>>;
```

Matching `Promise<infer V>` passes the first three and is the wrong answer: a
library's thenable is not a `Promise`, and `await` does not care.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"Thenable" is a structural claim: an object with a `then` method whose first
parameter is a callback. Write that as a type and you have your pattern - the
`infer` goes on the callback's parameter, two levels in.

## Hint 2

You can `infer` through nested function types. Here is the same idea on a
callback-style API:

```ts
type NodeResult<F> =
  F extends (cb: (err: Error | null, value: infer V) => void) => void ? V : never;
```

Nothing special is happening: the pattern is just a type, and `infer` can sit
anywhere inside it.

## Hint 3

Three branches, in this order: nullish passes through unchanged, thenable
recurses on the inferred value, anything else is already settled.

Left to you: what to put in the `then` pattern for the parameters you do not
care about. `...rest: never[]` and `...rest: any[]` behave differently against
real `PromiseLike` declarations - try one, read the failure, and keep the one
that matches.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the assertion that will break first. `Settled<Promise<string> | number>`
distributes, so your conditional runs twice: once on `Promise<string>`, once on
`number`. If you get `string | number` you have both branches right. If you get
`never` for the number half, your fallback branch is returning `never` instead
of `T`.

## Hint 2

Look at how the standard library declares it. In `lib.es5.d.ts`:

```ts
type Awaited<T> = T extends null | undefined ? T :
  T extends object & { then(onfulfilled: infer F, ...args: infer _): any } ?
    F extends ((value: infer V, ...args: infer _) => any) ? Awaited<V> : never :
  T;
```

Yours does not need to be that defensive, but the *shape* - nullish first,
thenable second, passthrough last - is the shape to copy.

## Hint 3

Write it as a single type alias with two nested conditionals and a recursive
call in the middle branch. Four lines.

Left to you: whether to include the `object &` guard the standard library uses.
Work out what it protects against - think about a `string` and a union with
`any` in it - and decide whether this gate can tell the difference.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Mutual assignability is not equality, so a solution built out of two `extends`
checks cannot work no matter how you arrange it. You need to get the checker to
compare two types by *identity* instead. The only construct that does that is
the deferred conditional type.

## Hint 2

A conditional type over an unresolved type parameter is not evaluated - it is
stored and compared structurally to other deferred conditionals. So put `A` and
`B` inside two otherwise identical generic function types whose return types are
deferred conditionals, and ask whether one is assignable to the other:

```ts
type Same<A, B> = (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends /* the same, with B */
  ? true : false;
```

`Expect<T extends true>` is then trivial: a type alias whose constraint does the
asserting.

## Hint 3

`Equal` is one line, `NotEqual` is one line built on `Equal`, and `Expect` is a
constrained alias with no body worth speaking of.

Left to you: whether `NotEqual` should be `Equal<A, B> extends true ? false : true`
or the negation written out again from scratch. One of them stays correct if you
ever change `Equal`; write that one.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Run the experiment that motivates the whole exercise:

```ts
type Naive<A, B> = A extends B ? (B extends A ? true : false) : false;
type P1 = Naive<{ a?: string }, { a: string | undefined }>;   // true - wrong
type P2 = Naive<any, string>;                                 // boolean - wrong
```

Now you know exactly which two failures your implementation has to avoid, and
you can test against them as you go.

## Hint 2

The `any` failure is the empty-union rule's cousin: `any` satisfies both
branches of a distributive conditional, so any test built from `extends` returns
`boolean` for it. The optionality failure is different - the two object types
really are mutually assignable, and no assignability-based test can separate
them. Only identity can.

## Hint 3

Two generic function types, identical except for the type each one compares
against, and an `extends` between them. The `1` and `2` are arbitrary - what
matters is that the two branches differ.

Left to you: whether `Expect` should be `type Expect<T extends true> = T` or
something that also returns a useful value. Look at how the gate uses it before
you decide.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge - UnionToTuple

Turning a union into a tuple needs three of this sector's ideas at once:
`UnionToIntersection`, inference against an intersection of function types, and
a recursion with an accumulator.

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export type UnionToIntersection<U> = /* as in ex4 */;
export type LastOf<U> = /* the last member of the union */;
export type UnionToTuple<U, Acc extends unknown[] = []> = /* ... */;
```

Expected:

```ts
type _1 = Expect<Equal<UnionToTuple<"a" | "b" | "c">, ["a", "b", "c"]>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<UnionToTuple<never>, []>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<LastOf<"a" | "b">, "b">>;
```

The mechanism for `LastOf`: intersect a union of one-argument function types,
which produces an *overloaded* signature, then infer its parameter. Inference
against overloads picks the last signature - so you get the last union member.

Honest caveat, and part of the exercise: the order of union members is an
implementation detail of the checker, not a guarantee of the language. Real
libraries depend on it anyway. Know that you are doing so.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta01_conditional_types_infer challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three types, and the second one is the interesting one. `UnionToIntersection`
of a union of functions gives you `((x: A) => void) & ((x: B) => void)` - and an
intersection of function types is how TypeScript spells "overloaded". Ask that
overloaded type for its parameter with `infer` and see which one you get.

## Hint 2

The recursion is an accumulator loop, the same shape you would write in
JavaScript:

```ts
type Reverse<T extends unknown[], Acc extends unknown[] = []> =
  T extends [infer H, ...infer R] ? Reverse<R, [H, ...Acc]> : Acc;
```

Yours has no tuple to destructure - it has a union to shrink. Take the last
member off, prepend it to the accumulator, and recurse on what is left.

## Hint 3

The base case is `[U] extends [never] ? Acc : ...` - note the tuple wrap, or
the empty union will send you somewhere you did not intend. The step removes the
extracted member with `Exclude` and prepends it: `[LastOf<U>, ...Acc]`.

Left to you: whether to prepend or append. One of the two gives you declaration
order and the other reverses it, and the `["a", "b", "c"]` assertion decides
which one you wanted.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build it in three sittings, checking a hover after each.

1. `UnionToIntersection<((x: "a") => void) | ((x: "b") => void)>` - what does the
   hover say? You should see an intersection of two function types.
2. `... extends (x: infer L) => void ? L : never` applied to that - which member
   comes out?
3. Only then write the recursion.

Skipping to step 3 is how people spend an hour on this.

## Hint 2

The overload rule is the whole trick, and it is worth confirming in plain code
before you trust it in a type:

```ts
declare function f(x: "a"): void;
declare function f(x: "b"): void;
type P = Parameters<typeof f>;   // ["b"] - the last overload wins
```

An intersection of function types behaves exactly like that declaration.

## Hint 3

`LastOf` is `UnionToIntersection` applied to a distributively-built union of
functions, then a second conditional with `infer` in the parameter slot - so it
is ex4 plus one more step. `UnionToTuple` is a two-parameter recursive alias with
a defaulted accumulator.

Left to you: what `UnionToTuple<boolean>` should give. Work out what `boolean` is
made of before you predict it, then check.

# V3·TA2 — Mapped types and key remapping

`d14_mapped_types` taught you the syntax and had you rebuild `Partial`,
`Readonly` and `Pick`. Those are the easy ones, because they all map every key
to itself and change only the value type or a modifier. This sector is about
what happens when you start changing the *keys*, and about a property of mapped
types that has a name most TypeScript users never learn: **homomorphism**.

The reason to learn the name is that it is the difference between a `DeepPartial`
that works and one that turns every tuple in your codebase into an object with a
`push` method.

## Key remapping with `as`

TypeScript 4.1 added an `as` clause to the mapped type key position:

```ts
type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<K & string>}`]: () => T[K];
};

type G = Getters<{ id: string; open: boolean }>;
// { getId: () => string; getOpen: () => boolean }
```

Two things it can do, and only two. It can **rename** a key, usually with a
template literal type. And it can **remove** a key, by mapping it to `never`:

```ts
type PickByValue<T, V> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends V ? K : never]: T[K];
};
```

That is the whole feature. What makes it powerful is that the `as` expression is
an ordinary type expression, so every conditional type from the previous sector
is available inside it.

Two traps show up immediately. `K` is `string | number | symbol`, so template
literals need `K & string` — and that intersection is `never` for a symbol key,
which means **symbol keys silently disappear** from a renaming map. And a
property declared optional has `undefined` in its type, so `done?: boolean` does
*not* satisfy `T[K] extends boolean`; a value-based filter will drop it unless
you strip the optionality first.

## The modifier operators

```ts
type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type Concrete<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };
type Loose<T>    = { [K in keyof T]+?: T[K] };   // + is the default, rarely written
```

`-?` does two jobs and the second one surprises people: it removes the optional
marker *and* removes `undefined` from the property's type. That is deliberate —
`a?: string` really means `a?: string | undefined`, so removing the marker
without removing the `undefined` would leave you with a required property that
can still be `undefined`. But it also means `-?` cannot distinguish
`a?: string` from `a: string | undefined`: applied to the second, it leaves the
`undefined` alone.

## Homomorphism, and why you care

A mapped type is **homomorphic** when its key source is exactly `keyof T` for a
naked type parameter `T`:

```ts
type Clone<T>   = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] };                    // homomorphic
type Rebuilt<T> = { [K in Extract<keyof T, PropertyKey>]: T[K] };  // not
```

Those two look interchangeable. They are not. A homomorphic mapped type:

- **preserves `readonly` and `?`** unless you explicitly change them;
- **passes arrays and tuples through as arrays and tuples**, mapping the element
  types — `Clone<readonly string[]>` is `readonly string[]`, and
  `Clone<[a: 1, b?: 2]>` keeps both the labels and the optional slot;
- **distributes over a union**, so `Clone<{ a: 1 } | { b: 2 }>` is
  `{ a: 1 } | { b: 2 }` rather than a mapping over `keyof` of the union (which
  is `never`).

`Rebuilt<T>` does none of those. `Rebuilt<{ readonly a?: string }>` is
`{ a: string | undefined }`: modifiers gone, and an array argument comes back as
a plain object with `push` and `length` as properties.

An `as` clause does **not** break homomorphism — the key source is still
`keyof T`. Computing the key source with anything else does.

This is the mechanism behind the most-complained-about type in the standard
library. `Omit<T, K>` is defined as `Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>`, and `Pick`
maps over `K`, not over `keyof T`. So `Omit` is not homomorphic, which is why

```ts
type Bad = Omit<{ a: 1 } | { b: 2 }, "c">;   // {}
```

collapses a union to nothing instead of removing `"c"` from each member. You
will write the replacement in ex5.

## `Prettify`, the identity map that earns its keep

```ts
type Prettify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {};
```

It computes nothing. It exists so that an intersection like
`{ a: 1 } & { b: 2 }` is displayed — and compared — as `{ a: 1; b: 2 }`. Every
library that composes types with `&` ships one of these, usually under the name
`Simplify` or `Id`. The `& {}` at the end is what forces the checker to
normalise the result rather than keeping it lazy.

Rename every key, and find out what happens to a `symbol` key.

```

```

## ex2 — filter keys by value type

```

```

## ex3 — the modifier operators

```

```

## ex4 — homomorphic or not

differently on tuples, modifiers and unions.

```

```

## ex5 — a better `Omit`

`Except<T, K>` that preserves modifiers and rejects unknown keys, and a
`DistributiveExcept` that survives a discriminated union.

```

```

## ex6 — mapping across a union

`AllKeys<T>` and a `Squashed<T>` that gives every member the same key set.

```

```

## ex7 — deleting an index signature

config object.

```

```

```

```

## Challenge — a generated store API

# Reading - typescript/v3ta02_mapped_types_remapping

## Notes

**A mapped type is a loop, and `as` is the only place you may change the key.**
Everything else in the header — the modifiers, the constraint — controls how the
loop runs. The body controls the value. Once you see it as
`for (K of keyof T) { key = as-expression; value = body }`, the feature stops
being mysterious and the remaining questions are all about what the compiler
does around the loop.

**Homomorphism is a property of the key source, nothing else.** `keyof T` where
`T` is a naked type parameter: homomorphic. `keyof T` plus an `as` clause: still
homomorphic. Anything else — `Extract<keyof T, string>`, `keyof T & string`, a
key union computed by a helper, or a concrete `keyof SomeInterface` — is not.
The consequences are large and silent: modifiers are dropped, tuples and arrays
turn into plain objects, and unions stop distributing.

**`-?` removes `undefined` as well as the marker.** This is the right default and
it is also a small information loss: after `Concrete<T>`, a property that was
`a?: string` and one that was `a: string` are indistinguishable, while
`b: number | undefined` keeps its `undefined` because there was no optional
marker to remove. If you need "required but may be undefined", write it out.

**`K & string` is how you get into a template literal, and it is also a filter.**
For a `string` key it is the key; for a `symbol` key it is `never`, and a
template literal containing `never` is `never`, so the property vanishes. That is
occasionally what you want and usually a bug you did not notice. If symbol keys
matter, handle them in the `as` clause explicitly.

**Optional properties defeat naive value filters.** `T[K]` for `done?: boolean`
is `boolean | undefined`, which does not extend `boolean`. Either use
`NonNullable<T[K]> extends V` or apply `-?` first, and decide which one you meant
rather than discovering it in a code review.

**`Omit` is the standard library's most-reported design wart.** It is not
homomorphic, it accepts keys that do not exist on `T` (so a typo silently omits
nothing), and it collapses unions. The three-line replacement in ex5 fixes the
first two; the distributive wrapper fixes the third. Most large codebases have
both under some name.

**`Prettify` is not cosmetic when types are compared.** An intersection and the
flattened object are assignable to each other but are different types, so a
`Equal`-style assertion, an error message, and a hover all see the difference.
Flattening at the boundary of a public API is a kindness to whoever hovers it.

## ex1 — Getters

The exercise is one line, and the assertion about symbol keys is the lesson. If
your renaming map is applied to a type with symbol keys, they disappear without
a word. That is a real bug pattern: a library adds a `[Symbol.toStringTag]`
member and half your derived type quietly changes shape.

## ex2 — PickByValue

Two ideas: filtering by mapping to `never`, and the fact that a filter written
over `T[K]` sees the *declared* type including `undefined`. The
`PickByValue<Row, boolean>` assertion coming back as `{}` for an optional
`done?: boolean` is the whole point; it is not a mistake in the gate.

## ex3 — Mutable and Concrete

Straightforward until the second assertion. `Concrete<{ b: number | undefined }>`
keeps the `undefined` because `-?` only strips the `undefined` that the optional
marker implies. Say that sentence back to yourself with `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`
in mind and you will understand why that flag exists.

## ex4 — homomorphic or not

The point of the exercise is that you can see, in three assertions, the whole
cost of writing the key source the wrong way. `Rebuilt` loses `readonly` and
`?`, turns `readonly string[]` into something that is no longer an array type,
and stops distributing. Nothing about that is documented in the syntax; the only
defence is knowing the rule.

## ex5 — Except

Constraining `K extends keyof T` is what makes a typo an error rather than a
silent no-op, and it is the reason to prefer your own type over `Omit` in
application code. The distributive version needs `K extends PropertyKey`
instead, because `keyof T` for a union is the intersection of the members' keys —
usually just the discriminant, and often `never`.

## ex6 — AllKeys and Squashed

Two conditional types wrapped around a mapped type, and one subtlety worth the
whole exercise: once the outer conditional distributes, `T` inside it is a single
member, so `AllKeys<T>` computed there returns that member's keys. The key set
has to be captured *before* the distribution — which is what the defaulted second
type parameter is for. Defaulted parameters as "let bindings" is a technique you
will use again in the recursion sector.

## ex7 — RemoveIndex

An index signature makes `keyof T` include `string` (or `number`, or `symbol`),
which makes autocomplete useless and `Object.keys`-shaped helpers untypeable. The
filter works because `string extends K` is true only for the index signature's
own key, never for a literal key. Three tests, one per index signature kind.

## ex8 — Prettify and Merge

`Merge` is where `Prettify` stops being about looks: `Omit<A, keyof B> & B` is
correct and unreadable, and the flattened version is correct and obvious. The
assertion that `Merge<{ a: string; b?: number }, { b: string }>` has a
*required* `b: string` is the one to think about — `B`'s declaration wins
completely, modifiers included.

## challenge — the generated store

The type half is three mapped types intersected and flattened. The runtime half
is the part worth doing: you cannot build those keys without a loop, the loop
cannot be typed precisely, and the honest solution is to build a
`Record<string, unknown>` and cast once at the return. That is the standard
shape for "the types are computed, the implementation is dynamic" — and writing
the cast yourself, at a boundary you chose, is very different from sprinkling
`any`.

## review1 — filters

Two mapped types over the same source, each renaming keys differently, unioned by
intersection and flattened. It also adds `?` to keys that were required in the
source, which is the direction people forget is available. `SortSpec` then
reuses the ex2 filter idea in a domain where it is genuinely useful: you can sort
by a `Date` and not by an arbitrary object.

# V3·TA2 — Mapped types and key remapping (archive)

## 1. Anatomy

```ts
type Example<T> = {
  readonly [K in keyof T as NewKey<K>]?: Value<T[K]>;
//  ^modifier   ^binding  ^source ^rename  ^optional  ^value
};
```

- **modifier position**: `readonly`, `-readonly`, or nothing.
- **binding**: the type variable for the current key.
- **source**: the union of keys to iterate. This is the field that decides
  homomorphism.
- **rename**: optional `as` clause, TypeScript 4.1+. Map to `never` to delete.
- **optional position**: `?`, `-?`, `+?`, or nothing.
- **value**: any type expression, usually involving `T[K]`.

## 2. Homomorphism, stated precisely

A mapped type is homomorphic when the source is `keyof T` and `T` is a type
parameter. An `as` clause does not change this.

| written as | homomorphic | preserves `?`/`readonly` | arrays/tuples pass through | distributes over unions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `{ [K in keyof T]: X }` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `{ [K in keyof T as F<K>]: X }` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `{ [K in Extract<keyof T, string>]: X }` | no | no | no | no |
| `{ [K in keyof T & string]: X }` | no | no | no | no |
| `{ [K in Keys]: X }` for a computed `Keys` | no | no | no | no |

Worked demonstration:

```ts
type Clone<T>   = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type Rebuilt<T> = { [K in Extract<keyof T, PropertyKey>]: T[K] };

type C1 = Clone<readonly string[]>;          // readonly string[]
type C2 = Clone<[a: 1, b?: 2]>;              // [a: 1, b?: 2]
type C3 = Clone<{ readonly a?: string }>;    // { readonly a?: string }
type C4 = Clone<{ a: 1 } | { b: 2 }>;        // { a: 1 } | { b: 2 }

type R3 = Rebuilt<{ readonly a?: string }>;  // { a: string | undefined }
```

If you take one table out of this sector, take that one.

## 3. Renaming patterns

```ts
// prefix + capitalise
type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<K & string>}`]: () => T[K] };

// suffix
type Events<T> = { [K in keyof T as `${K & string}Changed`]: (v: T[K]) => void };

// two keys per source key: intersect two maps
type Filters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `${K & string}_eq`]?: T[K] } &
                  { [K in keyof T as `${K & string}_in`]?: readonly T[K][] };

// delete
type Public<T> = { [K in keyof T as K extends `_${string}` ? never : K]: T[K] };
```

A single mapped type cannot produce two keys from one source key — the `as`
expression yields one key per iteration — so the two-keys case is two maps and an
intersection (plus `Prettify` if anyone will read it).

## 4. Common mistakes

**Filtering on `T[K]` without accounting for optionality.**
`{ done?: boolean }` has `T["done"] = boolean | undefined`. Use
`NonNullable<T[K]> extends V` if you meant "the declared value type ignoring
optionality".

**Forgetting `& string` — or forgetting what it costs.** Without it, a template
literal over `K` is an error. With it, symbol keys are silently dropped.

**Using `keyof T & string` as the key source.** It looks like a harmless filter
and it silently makes your mapped type non-homomorphic. Filter in the `as`
clause instead: `[K in keyof T as K extends string ? K : never]`.

**Assuming `Omit` behaves like a mapped type.** It does not distribute, does not
check that the omitted key exists, and is not homomorphic.

**Mapping over a union's `keyof`.** `keyof ({ a: 1 } | { b: 2 })` is `never`,
because only keys present on every member are safe to read. If you want per
member behaviour, distribute first.

**Deriving a type from a mapped type inside a conditional and expecting the key
set of the whole union.** After distribution, `T` is one member. Capture what you
need in a defaulted type parameter before distributing.

## 5. Interview answer

> A mapped type iterates a key union and produces an object type. Since 4.1 you
> can remap the key with `as`, which lets you rename keys with template literal
> types or delete them by mapping to `never`. The subtlety worth knowing is
> homomorphism: when the key source is literally `keyof T` for a type parameter,
> the mapped type preserves `readonly` and `?`, passes arrays and tuples through,
> and distributes over unions. Compute the key source any other way and you lose
> all three silently — which is exactly why `Omit`, defined as `Pick` over
> `Exclude<keyof T, K>`, collapses unions and drops modifiers.

## 6. Performance notes

Mapped types are usually cheap: one instantiation per key. The costs come from
what you put in them.

- A conditional type in the `as` clause runs once per key. A conditional type in
  the value runs once per key. A conditional type in both, over a 200-key
  interface, is 400 instantiations per use of the alias.
- Renaming with template literals over large key unions produces large string
  unions; combine two of those and you can reach the checker's union size limit.
- Intersections of many mapped types are slow to display and slow to compare;
  `Prettify` costs one more pass but usually pays for itself in every downstream
  comparison.
- A homomorphic mapped type over a union distributes, so its cost is
  multiplied by the number of members. This is easy to miss because the syntax
  does not change.

## 7. A worked example: props that follow the element

The pattern that pays for this whole sector, from any component library:

```ts
type Prettify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {};

type OwnProps = { variant: "primary" | "ghost"; loading?: boolean };

type ButtonProps = Prettify<
  Omit<React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>, keyof OwnProps> & OwnProps
>;
```

Read it right to left: take everything a `<button>` accepts, remove anything this
component redefines, add this component's own props, and flatten so that an error
message names one object instead of an intersection of two. Every part of that is
something you wrote in this sector.

The variant that goes wrong, and why:

```ts
// Loses readonly and optional markers on the element's own props.
type Bad = { [K in Extract<keyof Attrs, string>]: Attrs[K] } & OwnProps;

// Collapses to {} if Attrs is ever a union of element attribute types.
type Worse = Omit<Attrs, keyof OwnProps> & OwnProps;   // fine until Attrs is a union
```

The second one is the bug you will actually ship, because it works for a year and
then someone types a polymorphic `as` prop and `Attrs` becomes a union.

## 8. Check yourself

1. What are the only two things an `as` clause can do?
2. Define homomorphic in one sentence, without using the word "mapped".
3. Why does `Clone<[a: 1, b?: 2]>` keep its labels but `Rebuilt` does not?
4. What does `-?` do beyond removing the question mark?
5. Why does `PickByValue<{ done?: boolean }, boolean>` come back empty?
6. What happens to symbol keys in `` `get${Capitalize<K & string>}` ``?
7. Give two reasons to prefer a hand-written `Except<T, K extends keyof T>` over
   `Omit`.
8. What is `keyof ({ a: 1 } | { b: 2 })`, and why?
9. Write the mapped type that strips a `[key: string]: unknown` index signature.
10. Why can a single mapped type not produce two keys per source key, and what do
    you do instead?
11. What does `& {}` add to `{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`?
12. When is a mapped type over a union evaluated once, and when once per member?
13. How would you filter to string keys only *without* losing homomorphism?
