# Reading - typescript/v3ta04_recursive_types_depth

## Notes

**There are two ceilings and they are twenty times apart.** Measured on 5.9.3: a
recursive conditional whose call is nested inside a construct fails at 49 levels;
one whose call is the entire true branch fails at 1000. Everything else in this
sector follows from that gap. If a recursive type of yours reports TS2589 on
input that is not absurd, the fix is almost always the accumulator rewrite, not
a smaller input.

**Tail position means literally nothing wraps the call.** `Concat<R, Acc>` in
the true branch is tail position. `` `${Concat<R>}x` `` is not. `[...Concat<R>]`
is not. `Wrapper<Concat<R>>` is not. The optimisation was added in TypeScript
4.5 and it is purely syntactic: the checker rewrites the recursion into a loop
when it can see that no work remains.

**Accumulators are how you get into tail position.** Add a second type parameter
with a default, do the combining step *before* the recursive call, and return the
accumulator in the base case. The same transformation you would apply to a
recursive JavaScript function you were about to blow the stack with.

**Structural recursion is free; evaluative recursion is not.** `type Json = ... |
Json[] | { [k: string]: Json }` is fine because the checker never has to expand
it eagerly. A conditional type that refers to itself must be evaluated, and every
evaluation is an instantiation the compiler counts.

**A deep utility is a list of exceptions.** The mapped type is the easy part.
`Date`, `RegExp`, `Map`, `Set`, functions, class instances and arrays each need a
branch, and the order matters because the first matching branch wins. Writing
`T extends object ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: ... }` first makes every other
branch unreachable.

**Bounded recursion is a design choice, not a workaround.** `Paths<T>` with a
depth of 3 is more useful in an editor than an unbounded one that takes 400ms per
keystroke, and it cannot be crashed by a self-referential type. Pick a limit,
document it, expose it as a parameter.

**TS2589 is not always about depth.** It also appears when a recursion does not
consume input — an empty separator, a pattern that matches without shortening the
string. Before rewriting for tail position, check that each step strictly
reduces something.

## ex1 — LengthOf

The canonical accumulator, and the one place a tuple is used purely as a counter:
`Acc["length"]` is how you get a numeric literal out of the type system, because
there is no arithmetic. Notice that this makes counting O(n) instantiations, and
that the maximum length you can count to is the tail-recursion limit.

## ex2 — Repeat

`Acc["length"] extends N` as the base case is worth staring at: it compares a
numeric literal to `N`, so it only terminates when `N` is a literal. `Repeat<T,
number>` never matches and runs to the limit — a good thing to try once so that
the error message becomes familiar rather than alarming.

## ex3 — Reverse

Both reversals are the same algorithm. The tuple version shows why the
accumulator is prepended rather than appended, and the string version shows the
same idea with template literal concatenation. The `readonly` input assertion is
there to remind you that `readonly [Head, ...Rest]` in the pattern accepts both
kinds of tuple.

## ex4 — the TS2589 fix

The exercise is the rewrite, and the diagnostic value is in doing it to code you
did not write. The starting version is correct and readable and fails at 49
elements; yours should be correct, slightly less readable, and good to a
thousand. That trade is the whole reason to know the rule.

## ex5 — DeepReadonly

Six branches, and each one is a bug that a three-line implementation would have.
The `Map` branch is the one most implementations skip: mapping over a `Map`'s
properties gives you an object with readonly method properties that still mutate
the underlying map. `ReadonlyMap` is the honest answer.

## ex6 — DeepPartial

The array decision is the interesting one. `DeepPartial<{ rows: { id: string }[] }>`
could make the elements optional (`(T | undefined)[]`), or make the array
optional, or make each element deep-partial. The gate wants the last, which is
what every configuration-merging library does — and being able to say why is
better than knowing the answer.

## ex7 — Json

The type is four tokens of recursion and needs no special handling, which is the
point: this is what the checker can do lazily. The validator is where the
subtleties live — `typeof null === "object"`, `NaN` and `Infinity` are numbers
that `JSON.stringify` turns into `null`, and an object with a `toJSON` method is
not what its own type says it is.

## ex8 — Paths

`Prev` as a decrement table is the standard trick for bounded type-level
recursion, and the `[D] extends [never]` base case is the previous sector's
distribution rule earning its place. The array exclusion is a design decision:
`tags.0.length` is expressible but rarely what an autocomplete user wants.

## challenge — DeepGet

`DeepGet` plus `getIn` is the pattern that makes deep-path helpers safe, and it
is also a clean example of the boundary cast. The type computes the result
precisely; the implementation walks an unknown object with a loop and casts once
at the return, because no amount of generic gymnastics will let the checker
follow a `for` loop over a dotted string.

## review1 — trees

A tree is the recursive structure everyone actually has, and the three types
around it exercise three different techniques: `Leaves` recurses through an
`infer`red element type, `Depth` counts with an accumulator, and `collect`
demonstrates that the runtime recursion is trivial while the type-level one
needed thought.

# V3·TA4 — Recursive types and the depth limits (archive)

## 1. The measurements

TypeScript 5.9.3, default settings. Reproduce them before you trust them.

| shape | limit | error |
|---|---|---|
| recursive call nested inside a construct | 48 levels ok, 49 fails | TS2589 |
| recursive call in tail position | 999 ok, 1000 fails | TS2589 |
| recursion through an object or array type only | no limit | — |
| self-reference with nothing to defer (`type A = A`) | immediate | TS2456 |

The probe used for the first two:

```ts
type Build<N extends number, Acc extends unknown[] = []> =
  Acc["length"] extends N ? Acc : Build<N, [...Acc, unknown]>;

type NonTail<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [unknown, ...infer R] ? [unknown, ...NonTail<R>] : [];

type Tail<T extends unknown[], Acc extends unknown[] = []> =
  T extends [unknown, ...infer R] ? Tail<R, [...Acc, unknown]> : Acc;
```

## 2. Turning a recursion into a tail recursion

The mechanical steps:

1. Add a parameter for the result so far, with a default that is the identity
   value (`[]`, `""`, `{}`).
2. Move the combining operation from around the recursive call to the argument
   of the recursive call.
3. Return the accumulator in the base case instead of the identity value.
4. Check the direction: prepending and appending are not the same, and the
   accumulator version often reverses the order the naive one produced.

Applied to `Reverse`, which is the easy case because the reversal is free:

```ts
type Reverse<T extends readonly unknown[], Acc extends unknown[] = []> =
  T extends readonly [infer H, ...infer R] ? Reverse<R, [H, ...Acc]> : Acc;
```

Applied to `Join`, where you must be careful about the separator:

```ts
type Join<T extends readonly string[], D extends string, Acc extends string = ""> =
  T extends readonly [infer H extends string, ...infer R extends string[]]
    ? Join<R, D, Acc extends "" ? H : `${Acc}${D}${H}`>
    : Acc;
```

## 3. The deep utility checklist

Any `Deep*<T>` needs a decision for each of these, in this order:

```ts
type Primitive = string | number | boolean | bigint | symbol | null | undefined;

type Deep<T> =
  T extends Primitive                        ? /* pass through */ :
  T extends (...args: never[]) => unknown    ? /* pass through - do not map a function */ :
  T extends Date | RegExp                    ? /* pass through - built-ins are opaque */ :
  T extends ReadonlyMap<infer K, infer V>    ? /* rebuild as a Map type */ :
  T extends ReadonlySet<infer V>             ? /* rebuild as a Set type */ :
  T extends readonly (infer E)[]             ? /* decide: elements, or the array itself */ :
  /* object */                                 /* the mapped type, recursing on values */;
```

Skipping the function branch is the most common bug: `DeepPartial` applied to a
config object with a callback turns `(x: number) => void` into `{}`, and the
error message that results points at the call site, not at the type.

## 4. Bounded recursion

```ts
type Prev = [never, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8];

type Paths<T, D extends number = 3> =
  [D] extends [never] ? never :
  T extends object ? { [K in keyof T & string]: K | `${K}.${Paths<T[K], Prev[D]>}` }[keyof T & string] :
  never;
```

Three details:

- `[D] extends [never]` must be tuple-wrapped, or the empty union distributes and
  the whole type collapses.
- `Prev` is a lookup table, because there is no subtraction. For larger limits,
  generate the table with `BuildTuple` or accept a tuple parameter directly.
- Bounding is not only about termination. It is about editor latency: an
  unbounded `Paths` over a Prisma-style generated type will make autocomplete
  unusable.

## 5. Type-level arithmetic, and why it stops

Everything numeric in the type system is a tuple length, so every operation is a
tuple operation:

```ts
type Add<A extends number, B extends number> =
  [...BuildTuple<A>, ...BuildTuple<B>]["length"];

type Sub<A extends number, B extends number> =
  BuildTuple<A> extends [...BuildTuple<B>, ...infer Rest] ? Rest["length"] : never;

type LessThan<A extends number, B extends number> =
  BuildTuple<B> extends [...BuildTuple<A>, unknown, ...unknown[]] ? true : false;
```

Each of those builds tuples of the operands' sizes, so the cost is linear in the
*values*, not in the number of digits. `Add<400, 400>` is fine; `Add<40000,
40000>` is not a slow type, it is an error. Multiplication is a nested recursion
and hits the wall almost immediately.

This is worth knowing mostly so you can recognise when a design has drifted. A
type that needs to add two numbers is usually a type that should have been a
value, and the next sectors offer better tools for the problems that tempt you
here.

## 6. Common mistakes

**Assuming the limit is a bug.** It is a defence. A checker with no depth limit
hangs on a type that recurses forever, and there is no way to prove in general
that a type-level program halts.

**Recursing without consuming.** An empty separator, a pattern that can match
zero characters, a decrement that does not decrement. Name the decreasing
quantity for every recursion you write.

**Wrapping the call "just a little".** `[...Recurse<R>]` looks like tail position
and is not; the spread is a construct around the call. So is
`` `${Recurse<R>}` ``.

**Mapping over a class instance.** Private fields do not survive a mapped type,
so `DeepReadonly<SomeClass>` produces something that is not assignable to
`SomeClass` and gives a confusing error.

**Forgetting that `Acc["length"] extends N` needs a literal.** Passing `number`
runs to the ceiling.

**Deep utilities in a public API.** Every consumer's hover now expands the whole
recursion. Alias the result for the common cases.

## 7. Interview answer

> TypeScript's type system is a total language only because it has recursion
> limits. There are two: about fifty instantiations deep when the recursive call
> is nested inside a construct, and a thousand when it is in tail position,
> because 4.5 added tail-recursion elimination for conditional types. So the
> standard technique is to carry an accumulator so the recursive call is the
> whole branch. Recursion through object or array types — like the classic `Json`
> type — is different: it is lazy and unbounded, because the checker never has to
> expand it eagerly. And for things like a `Paths<T>` helper you bound the depth
> deliberately with a decrement tuple, both to guarantee termination and to keep
> the editor responsive.

## 8. Check yourself

1. What are the two depth limits, and what distinguishes the shapes they apply
   to?
2. Why is `[...Recurse<R>]` not tail position?
3. Write `Reverse` with an accumulator and say which end the accumulator grows
   from.
4. Why does `type Json = ... | Json[]` compile while `type A = A` does not?
5. Name three types that a naive `DeepReadonly` breaks.
6. What does `Prev[D]` do, and why must the base case be tuple-wrapped?
7. What is `Repeat<"x", number>` and why?
8. What are two distinct causes of TS2589?
9. How do you get a numeric literal out of a tuple, and what does that cost?
10. Why does mapping over a class instance produce something unassignable to the
    class?
11. When would you deliberately choose the non-tail-recursive version?
12. What does `--generateTrace` tell you that `--extendedDiagnostics` does not?

# Reading - typescript/v3ta04_recursive_types_depth (long form)

## How the limits came to exist

The type checker is a program that must terminate. Since TypeScript's type-level
language is expressive enough to encode arbitrary computation — it is Turing
complete, a fact demonstrated repeatedly with type-level SKI combinators and
Turing machines — no analysis can decide in general whether a given type
evaluation halts. The compiler team's answer was blunt and correct: count
instantiations, and give up past a threshold with a diagnostic that says what
happened.

That is TS2589, "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite".
The wording is careful: *possibly* infinite. The compiler does not know whether
your type would have terminated; it knows it went further than any reasonable
type should.

TypeScript 3.7 (November 2019) is the release that made this a common concern,
because it permitted recursive type aliases to be referenced in more positions —
before that, the `Json` type had to be written as an interface plus a union, and
recursive conditional types were largely impossible. 4.1 (November 2020)
explicitly enabled recursive conditional types and shipped the first practical
string manipulation utilities. 4.5 (November 2021) added tail-recursion
elimination, which raised the effective ceiling from roughly fifty to a thousand
for types written in the right shape.

That last change is worth appreciating. Nothing about the type system's
semantics changed; the checker simply recognised a pattern — the true branch of
a conditional type being nothing but a recursive reference to the same type — and
evaluated it iteratively instead of recursively. The same optimisation every
functional language compiler performs, arriving in a type checker.

## How the checker counts

Two counters matter. The instantiation depth counter tracks how deeply nested the
current type instantiation is; the total instantiation counter tracks how many
types have been created for the whole program. The depth counter is what produces
TS2589 for a runaway recursion. The total counter is what produces the *other*
failure mode: no error at all, just a build that takes four minutes.

`tsc --extendedDiagnostics` prints both, and the line to watch is
`Instantiations`. For a healthy medium-sized project it is in the hundreds of
thousands; a single badly written deep utility applied across a codebase can add
millions. `--generateTrace out/` goes further, writing a Chrome trace that
attributes time to individual type instantiations, which is the only reliable way
to find *which* alias is responsible when several are suspects.

There is a third, less discussed consequence of recursion: **error message
size**. A recursive type that fails to match produces an error containing the
expanded type, and expansion of a deep recursive type produces walls of text with
`...` elisions in the wrong places. Bounded recursion and named intermediate
aliases both improve this substantially, and for a library that is a user-facing
feature.

## Structural versus evaluative recursion, in the checker

```ts
type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [key: string]: Json };
```

When the checker resolves this alias, it creates a union type whose members
include an array type and an index-signature object type, both of whose element
types are *the alias itself*. That is a cycle in the type graph, and the checker
is built to handle cycles in the type graph — it resolves lazily and memoises.
Nothing is expanded until something asks a question that requires expansion, and
questions like "is `{ a: 1 }` assignable to `Json`" are answered structurally, one
level at a time, with a cache to break the cycle.

```ts
type Expand<T> = T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]: Expand<T[K]> } : T;
```

This one is different. Applying `Expand` to a concrete type requires evaluating
the conditional, which requires instantiating the mapped type, which requires
evaluating `Expand` again for each property. Every one of those is counted.

The practical distinction: **if your recursive reference sits inside a type
constructor with no conditional between you and it, the recursion is free.** If a
conditional type has to be evaluated to reach the recursive reference, you are
spending instantiations and the limits apply.

## Reading a TS2589 without panic

The diagnostic points at the *use* of the type, not at the recursion, which makes
it feel less informative than it is. A method that works:

1. **Reduce the input.** Halve the tuple, shorten the string, take one field off
   the object. If the error disappears at some size, you have a depth problem and
   the accumulator rewrite is the fix. If it persists at size one, the recursion
   is not consuming input and no rewrite will help.
2. **Look for the wrapper.** Read the true branch of every conditional in the
   chain and ask whether the recursive reference is the whole branch. A spread, a
   template literal, an object type, another alias — any of them costs you the
   optimisation.
3. **Check the base case can be reached.** `Acc["length"] extends N` requires a
   literal `N`. A pattern that can match the empty string can loop forever. A
   decrement table that runs out gives `undefined`, not `never`, if you index past
   its end.
4. **Bound it.** If the recursion is genuinely unbounded — a self-referential
   object type, a path enumeration — add a depth parameter rather than hoping the
   inputs stay small.

The failure mode that is *not* an error deserves the same attention: a recursion
that stays under the limit but runs at every call site can add seconds to a build
without producing a single diagnostic. Instantiation counts, not error messages,
are how you find that one.

## When not to recurse

**When the data is deep and dynamic.** A `Paths<T>` over a generated database
client with a hundred tables and nested relations produces a union with tens of
thousands of members. It will technically compile and it will make the editor
unusable. Bound the depth, or expose the paths as a runtime array and validate
them.

**When the recursion is over user data rather than developer data.** The same
rule as the string sector: type-level recursion over a shape you control is
engineering, over a shape that arrives at runtime it is theatre.

**When a nominal wrapper would do.** If the reason you want `DeepReadonly` is to
stop one team mutating one object, a branded `Frozen<T>` type plus
`Object.freeze` is cheaper, clearer, and enforced at runtime as well. That is the
next sector's material and it is often the better answer.

**When the deep utility is applied at the boundary of a public API.** Every
consumer pays the instantiation cost, every hover shows the expansion, and every
error message includes it. Compute it once, alias the result, export the alias.

**When you have not measured.** The most common mistake with recursive types is
not writing one that is too slow; it is rewriting one that was never the problem.
`--extendedDiagnostics` before and after, every time.

## A closing rule of thumb

Recursive types are excellent for shapes: describing a tree, a JSON document, a
nested configuration. They are adequate for small computations over literals: a
path, a route, a version string. They are a poor choice for anything that
resembles a program with a stack.

The test that has served well: if you would need more than one accumulator to
write it in tail position, or if you find yourself building a lookup table for
arithmetic, you have left the domain where the type system is helping and entered
the one where it is a puzzle. The next sectors — variance, branded types — are
about tools that solve real problems with far less machinery, and knowing when to
reach for those instead is the more valuable skill.

```ts
type _1 = Expect<Equal<LengthOf<"hello">, 5>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<LengthOf<"">, 0>>;
```

The result must be the numeric *literal* `5`, not `number`. Getting a literal out
requires counting with a tuple and reading its `length`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Walk the string one character at a time, and for each character push
something - anything - onto a tuple. When the string is empty, the tuple's
`length` is your answer.

## Hint 2

The counter idiom, on a tuple input rather than a string:

```ts
type Count<T extends unknown[], Acc extends unknown[] = []> =
  T extends [unknown, ...infer R] ? Count<R, [...Acc, unknown]> : Acc["length"];
```

`Acc["length"]` on a tuple type is a numeric literal - the only way to produce
one without writing it down.

## Hint 3

One type, two parameters, one conditional. The accumulator's element type does
not matter; `unknown` is conventional.

Left to you: whether to consume the character with `` `${infer C}${infer R}` ``
or `` `${string}${infer R}` ``. You do not need the character - decide whether
capturing it anyway costs you anything.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask why the obvious approach is unavailable. `"hello"["length"]` is `number`,
not `5`, because the `length` of a `string` type is not tracked. Tuples are the
only structure whose length is part of its type, which is why every type-level
number in TypeScript is secretly a tuple.

## Hint 2

The accumulator's default is what makes the type callable with one argument:

```ts
type Count<S extends string, Acc extends unknown[] = []> = ...
```

Callers write `Count<"abc">`; the recursion writes `Count<"bc", [unknown]>`.
Defaulted parameters as internal state is the workhorse pattern of this whole
sector.

## Hint 3

Two lines. The base case returns `Acc["length"]`, the step recurses with one
more element.

Left to you: what happens for `LengthOf<string>` - not a literal, so the pattern
matches differently. Predict it, then check, and decide whether you want to guard
against it.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Grow a tuple until its length matches `N`. The base case is a comparison
between `Acc["length"]` and `N`, and the step appends one more element.

## Hint 2

The comparison in the base case is an ordinary conditional over literal types:

```ts
type Grow<N extends number, Acc extends unknown[] = []> =
  Acc["length"] extends N ? Acc : Grow<N, [...Acc, unknown]>;
```

Note that this only terminates when `N` is a numeric *literal*. `Grow<number>`
never matches and runs to the ceiling.

## Hint 3

`Repeat` is that type with an extra parameter for the element. `BuildTuple` is
`Repeat` with `unknown`.

Left to you: whether to constrain the accumulator as `T[]` or `unknown[]`. One
of them gives a nicer error when someone passes a mismatched accumulator by
hand; neither changes the result.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Try the failure on purpose once. Write the version that fails - for example by
wrapping the recursive call in a tuple - and feed it 400. Read the exact error
text and where it points. Recognising TS2589 on sight is worth more than any
particular type in this sector.

## Hint 2

This type is a primitive that everything else builds on. Type-level addition is
`[...BuildTuple<A>, ...BuildTuple<B>]["length"]`; subtraction is a tuple pattern
match; comparison is checking whether one tuple can be destructured to the other
length. All of it is O(n) instantiations, which is why type-level arithmetic
stops being practical in the low thousands.

## Hint 3

Two aliases, and the second is one line built from the first.

Left to you: whether `Repeat<T, number>` should be an error or a hang. You cannot
easily make it an error - but you can constrain `N` so that a caller gets a
better message. Decide whether it is worth it.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Take the head off the input and put it on the *front* of the accumulator. After
one pass the accumulator holds the input backwards, which is the answer.

## Hint 2

The tuple version's pattern accepts both mutable and readonly inputs if you
write it with `readonly`:

```ts
type Head<T> = T extends readonly [infer H, ...unknown[]] ? H : never;
```

A `readonly` pattern matches a mutable tuple as well; the reverse is not true,
which is why assertion 4 exists.

## Hint 3

Two types, two lines each. The string version's accumulator is a `string` with
a default of `""`, and the concatenation order is the mirror of the tuple
version's.

Left to you: whether `ReverseTuple` should return a `readonly` tuple when given
one. The gate wants a mutable tuple in both cases - decide whether you agree.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict the wrong version's output before you write the right one. If you
append to the accumulator instead of prepending - `[...Acc, Head]` - you get the
input back unchanged. Seeing that once makes "which end does the accumulator grow
from" a question you ask automatically.

## Hint 2

Reversal is the cheapest possible accumulator recursion, which makes it the
standard building block for the expensive ones. "Everything before the last
separator" is `Reverse`, split once, `Reverse` both halves. `Join` with a
separator only between elements is easier written on a reversed list. When a
recursion resists tail position, reversing first is often the unlock.

## Hint 3

Four lines total across two aliases.

Left to you: whether the string version should handle surrogate pairs - an emoji
is two UTF-16 code units, and this reversal will split it. The gate does not test
it; a production string utility has to decide.

references.solution.ts:
// v3ta04_recursive_types_depth / ex3 - reference solution (author only).

export type ReverseTuple<
  T extends readonly unknown[],
  Acc extends unknown[] = [],
> = T extends readonly [infer Head, ...infer Rest]
  ? ReverseTuple<Rest, [Head, ...Acc]>
  : Acc;

export type ReverseString<
  S extends string,
  Acc extends string = "",
> = S extends `${infer Head}${infer Rest}` ? ReverseString<Rest, `${Head}${Acc}`> : Acc;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - fix a TS2589

Here is a correct, readable type that fails on real input:

```ts
type ConcatSlow<T extends readonly string[]> =
  T extends readonly [infer H extends string, ...infer R extends string[]]
    ? `${H}${ConcatSlow<R>}`
    : "";
```

It works to about 48 elements and then reports
`error TS2589: Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite.`

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement a `Concat` with the same behaviour that handles
200 elements:

```ts
export type Concat<T extends readonly string[]> = /* ... */;
```

Expected:

```ts
type Long = Repeat<"x", 200>;

type _1 = Expect<Equal<Concat<["a", "b", "c"]>, "abc">>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<Concat<[]>, "">>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<LengthOf<Concat<Long>>, 200>>;
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta04_recursive_types_depth ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Look at where the recursive call sits in the failing version: inside a template
literal. Anything wrapped around the call means the checker has work left to do
after it returns, so it cannot turn the recursion into a loop.

## Hint 2

The transformation, in general form:

```ts
// before: combine after the call
type F<T> = T extends [infer H, ...infer R] ? Combine<H, F<R>> : Identity;

// after: combine before the call, carry the result down
type F<T, Acc = Identity> = T extends [infer H, ...infer R] ? F<R, Combine<Acc, H>> : Acc;
```

Note that the argument order to `Combine` flips: you are now building left to
right.

## Hint 3

One extra type parameter, defaulted to `""`, and the concatenation moves into
the recursive call's argument list.

Left to you: whether the accumulator goes first or second in the template
literal. Get it backwards and assertion 1 gives you `"cba"` - which is a useful
mistake to make once.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Confirm the failure boundary yourself before fixing it. Feed the slow version
tuples of 40, 48 and 49 elements. The transition is sharp, and knowing that the
number is around fifty rather than "some large number" changes how you read your
own types.

## Hint 2

Tail-recursion elimination landed in TypeScript 4.5 and is purely syntactic:
the checker looks at whether the true branch of the conditional is *only* a
reference to the same type. It does not analyse whether your recursion could have
been rewritten. That is your job, and it is the entire content of this
exercise.

## Hint 3

Two lines. The signature gains a defaulted parameter; the true branch loses its
template wrapper and gains an argument.

Left to you: whether to expose the accumulator in the public signature or hide it
behind a second alias. Exposing it is conventional and slightly leaky; hiding it
costs one more line.

references.solution.ts:
// v3ta04_recursive_types_depth / ex4 - reference solution (author only).

export type Concat<
  T extends readonly string[],
  Acc extends string = "",
> = T extends readonly [infer Head extends string, ...infer Rest extends string[]]
  ? Concat<Rest, `${Acc}${Head}`>
  : Acc;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This type is a chain of conditionals with the mapped type at the *end*. The
order is the specification: each branch removes a category of value that must
not be mapped over, and the object case catches whatever is left.

## Hint 2

The branches you need, in the order they must appear:

```ts
type Primitive = string | number | boolean | bigint | symbol | null | undefined;
//  primitive -> as is
//  function  -> as is        (mapping a function type destroys its signatures)
//  Date, RegExp -> as is     (built-ins with internal state)
//  Map, Set  -> the readonly variants, recursing on the type arguments
//  otherwise -> the readonly mapped type, recursing on each value
```

Arrays and tuples need no branch of their own - work out why before you add
one.

## Hint 3

Six branches, the last being
`{ readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }`.

Left to you: whether to match `Map` or `ReadonlyMap` in the pattern. One of them
also matches a `ReadonlyMap` input; the other does not, and getting it wrong
sends maps down the object branch.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the naive version first and hover the four failure cases. Seeing
`DeepReadonly<(x: number) => void>` come back as `{}` is more persuasive than
being told it happens - and the reason is worth knowing: a function type has no
enumerable properties, so mapping over `keyof` of it produces an empty object,
silently.

## Hint 2

The array question in hint 3: a homomorphic mapped type - one whose key source
is exactly `keyof T` - passes arrays and tuples through as arrays and tuples,
mapping the element type and applying the `readonly` modifier. That is the
previous sector's rule doing real work here, and it is why assertion 4 passes
without an array branch.

## Hint 3

One type alias, six branches, about a dozen lines with formatting.

Left to you: whether to add branches for `Promise`, `WeakMap` and typed arrays.
Each is a real type that the object branch would mangle. Decide where your
utility's contract ends and write it down.

references.solution.ts:
// v3ta04_recursive_types_depth / ex5 - reference solution (author only).

type Primitive = string | number | boolean | bigint | symbol | null | undefined;

export type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends Primitive
  ? T
  : T extends (...args: never[]) => unknown
    ? T
    : T extends Date | RegExp
      ? T
      : T extends ReadonlyMap<infer K, infer V>
        ? ReadonlyMap<DeepReadonly<K>, DeepReadonly<V>>
        : T extends ReadonlySet<infer V>
          ? ReadonlySet<DeepReadonly<V>>
          : { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> };

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## ex6 - DeepPartial

Same shape, different decisions - and the array decision is a real fork in the
road.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export type DeepPartial<T> = /* ... */;
```

Expected:

```ts
type _1 = Expect<Equal<DeepPartial<{ a: { b: string } }>, { a?: { b?: string } }>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<DeepPartial<{ when: Date }>, { when?: Date }>>;
type _3 = Expect<Equal<
  DeepPartial<{ rows: { id: string }[] }>["rows"],
  readonly { id?: string }[] | undefined
>>;
```

Assertion 3 says: the array becomes optional, its elements become deep-partial,
and it is handed back as a `readonly` array. Three separate decisions, all
defensible, all different from what a one-line implementation gives you.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta04_recursive_types_depth ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start from your ex5 answer and change two things: the modifier in the mapped
type becomes `?` instead of `readonly`, and the array case needs an explicit
branch this time.

## Hint 2

Why arrays need a branch here and did not in ex5: making every element of a
tuple optional is not the same as making the array's contents deep-partial. With
a homomorphic map you get

```ts
DeepPartial<{ rows: { id: string }[] }>   // { rows?: ({ id?: string } | undefined)[] }
```

with `undefined` inside the array - which says an element may be missing, not
that its fields may be. Usually not what a config merger wants.

## Hint 3

Five branches: primitive, function, `Date`, array, object. The array branch
rebuilds with `readonly DeepPartial<E>[]`.

Left to you: whether to keep the `Map`/`Set` branches from ex5. The gate does
not test them; a config type that contains a `Map` is not unusual.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Decide the semantics before you write anything, because there are three
plausible answers for arrays and they lead to different code:

1. the array itself is optional, contents unchanged;
2. the array is optional and each element is deep-partial;
3. the array is optional and each *slot* is optional.

The gate wants 2. Real merge libraries mostly want 2. Option 3 is what you get by
accident.

## Hint 2

`DeepPartial` is most often used for a config-merge function:

```ts
declare function merge<T>(base: T, overrides: DeepPartial<T>): T;
```

That signature is where the array decision shows up in practice - and it is also
where you discover that "merge" for arrays has no obvious meaning. Replace,
concatenate, or merge by index are all wrong in some codebase.

## Hint 3

Five branches, about ten lines.

Left to you: whether to also strip `readonly` while adding `?`. An overrides
object that must be deeply readonly is an odd requirement; a `DeepPartial` that
silently makes things mutable is an odd gift.

references.solution.ts:
// v3ta04_recursive_types_depth / ex6 - reference solution (author only).

type Primitive = string | number | boolean | bigint | symbol | null | undefined;

export type DeepPartial<T> = T extends Primitive
  ? T
  : T extends (...args: never[]) => unknown
    ? T
    : T extends Date
      ? T
      : T extends readonly (infer E)[]
        ? readonly DeepPartial<E>[]
        : { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> };

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - Json

The recursion that costs nothing, and the runtime check that makes it true.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export type Json = /* the JSON value type, recursively */;
export function isJson(value: unknown): value is Json;
```

Expected:

```ts
const doc: Json = { a: [1, "two", null, { b: true }] };   // assignable
isJson(() => 1);        // false
isJson({ a: [1] });     // true
```

The type is one line and needs no conditional type at all. The validator is where
the work is - and `typeof null === "object"`, `NaN` is a number that JSON cannot
represent, and `undefined` is not a JSON value.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta04_recursive_types_depth ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the type as a union of the JSON primitives plus an array of itself plus
an object whose values are itself. The self-references are inside an array type
and an index signature, which is why the checker accepts them without
complaint.

## Hint 2

Compare the two kinds of self-reference:

```ts
type Ok = string | Ok[];        // fine - behind an array
type No = No;                   // error: circularly references itself
type AlsoNo<T> = AlsoNo<T> extends string ? 1 : 2;   // must be evaluated
```

Recursion through a structure is lazy. Recursion through evaluation is counted,
and that is what the depth limits govern.

## Hint 3

The validator is a `typeof` chain with an `Array.isArray` branch and a recursive
`every` over the values.

Left to you: what to do about a non-finite number. `JSON.stringify(NaN)` produces
`null`, so a value that your type accepts may not survive a round trip - decide
whether your predicate should reject it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

List the traps before writing the function:

- `typeof null === "object"`, so the null check must come first;
- `typeof [] === "object"` too, so arrays need their own branch;
- `undefined` is not JSON, and neither is a function or a symbol;
- `NaN` and `Infinity` are numbers that `JSON.stringify` turns into `null`;
- an object with a `toJSON` method serialises as something else entirely.

Your predicate does not have to handle all of them, but it should handle the ones
you claim it does.

## Hint 2

This is the exercise where the type and the runtime meet honestly. `Json` is a
compile-time description; `isJson` is the only thing that makes it true for a
value that arrived over a network. A type predicate that returns `value is Json`
is a promise you are making to the compiler on the strength of the code you just
wrote - which is why the implementation deserves more care than its size
suggests.

## Hint 3

One type alias and a function of about ten lines with early returns.

Left to you: whether to guard against prototype pollution by rejecting objects
whose prototype is not `Object.prototype`. Parsed JSON never has a surprising
prototype; an object built in your own code might.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - depth-limited Paths

Every dotted path into an object type - with a deliberate ceiling.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export type Paths<T, D extends number = 3> = /* ... */;
```

Expected:

```ts
type Shape = { id: string; user: { name: string; address: { city: string } }; tags: string[] };

type _1 = Expect<Equal<
  Paths<Shape>,
  "id" | "user" | "user.name" | "user.address" | "user.address.city" | "tags"
>>;
```

Note what is *not* in that union: nothing under `tags`. Arrays stop the
recursion, because `tags.0.length` is expressible and almost never what an
autocomplete user wants.

The depth parameter must actually bound the recursion - a self-referential type
must not hang the compiler.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta04_recursive_types_depth ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two mechanisms. A mapped type over the string keys, immediately indexed by
`keyof T & string` to collapse it to a union - the key-filter idiom from earlier
sectors. And a counter parameter that decrements on each level.

## Hint 2

There is no subtraction, so decrementing is a lookup:

```ts
type Prev = [never, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8];
type Two = Prev[3];    // 2
type Stop = Prev[0];   // never
```

`never` at index 0 is what gives you a base case: check for it at the top of the
type and return `never`.

## Hint 3

The value of the mapped type is `K` for a leaf, and `K | `${K}.${Paths<T[K],
Prev[D]>}`` for a nested object. Arrays and functions count as leaves.

Left to you: whether the base-case check needs a tuple wrap. `D` is a naked type
parameter and the value you are comparing against is `never` - which should make
the answer immediate.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build it in the order the failures appear. First get one level working with no
depth parameter at all. Then add nesting and watch it work for `Shape`. Then
point it at a self-referential type:

```ts
type Node = { value: string; next: Node };
type P = Paths<Node>;
```

Without the counter this is where your editor stops responding. With it, you get
three levels and a type you can read.

## Hint 2

The depth parameter is not just a safety device, it is an ergonomic decision.
An unbounded `Paths` over a generated API client type produces a union with
thousands of members; the editor has to render all of them in an autocomplete
list, and it will visibly stall. Every library that ships this type bounds it,
usually between 3 and 6, and the good ones let you pass the bound.

## Hint 3

One alias, four or five branches, plus the `Prev` table.

Left to you: whether array indices should be included at all. `` `tags.${number}` ``
is expressible and is what a form library would need. Decide which product you
are building.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The type recurses on the *path*, not on the object: split off the segment
before the first dot, index into `T` with it, and recurse with the rest. The base
case is a path with no dot left.

## Hint 2

The two branches, in outline:

```ts
type Get<T, P extends string> =
  P extends `${infer K}.${infer Rest}` ? /* recurse into T[K] with Rest */ :
  P extends keyof T ? T[P] : undefined;
```

Each branch also has to handle the key not existing, which is what makes
assertion 2 pass instead of erroring.

## Hint 3

The implementation walks with a `let current: unknown` and returns
`current as DeepGet<T, P>` at the end, with an early return of
`undefined as DeepGet<T, P>` when a segment is missing.

Left to you: whether `getIn` should throw on a missing path instead of returning
`undefined`. The type says `undefined` is possible only when the path is wrong -
so a throw is defensible and changes the signature.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice that the recursion here is on the path, so its depth is the number of
segments - three or four in practice, nowhere near any limit. That is worth
seeing explicitly: not every recursive type is at risk, and knowing which of your
recursions are bounded by human-scale input tells you where not to spend
effort.

## Hint 2

A design alternative worth knowing: constrain `P` to `Paths<T>` from ex8.

```ts
declare function getIn<T extends object, P extends Paths<T>>(source: T, path: P): DeepGet<T, P>;
```

Now a wrong path is a compile error at the call site with a list of valid paths,
instead of a silent `undefined`. The cost is that `Paths<T>` has to be computed
for every call - which is exactly the editor-latency trade the previous exercise
warned about. Try it both ways.

## Hint 3

Two branches in the type, a six-line loop in the function, one cast on each
return.

Left to you: whether the loop should use `key in current` or a
`hasOwnProperty` check. They differ for inherited properties, and the type says
nothing about which you meant.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review - trees

The recursive structure you actually have in production, from three angles.

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export type Tree<T> = { value: T; children: readonly Tree<T>[] };

export type Leaves<T> = /* the union of values at nodes with no children */;
export type Depth<T> = /* the number of levels */;

export function collect<T>(tree: Tree<T>): T[];
```

Expected:

```ts
type _1 = Expect<Equal<Leaves<{ value: 1; children: readonly [] }>, 1>>;
type _2 = Expect<Equal<
  Depth<{ value: 1; children: readonly [{ value: 2; children: readonly [] }] }>,
  2
>>;

declare const tree: Tree<number>;
const values: number[] = collect(tree);   // pre-order, parents before children
```

`Tree<T>` itself needs no conditional type - it is structural recursion, and the
checker handles it lazily. The two derived types are evaluative recursion and are
subject to everything this sector measured.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3ta04_recursive_types_depth review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Leaves` asks two questions: does this node have an empty `children` tuple - if
so its value is a leaf - otherwise recurse into the element type of `children`.
Inferring that element type is one `infer` inside a pattern.

## Hint 2

Recursing into a union of children happens for free:

```ts
type Values<T> = T extends { children: readonly (infer C)[] } ? Values<C> : never;
```

If `children` is a tuple of several node types, `C` is the union of them, and the
conditional distributes - so one recursive call covers every child.

## Hint 3

`Depth` is a counter: an accumulator tuple that grows by one per level, with the
empty-children case returning the length.

Left to you: whether `Depth` of a single leaf node should be `1` or `0`.
Assertion 2 pins the two-level case; decide what the one-level case means before
you write the base case.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Try `Leaves<Tree<number>>` - the general type, not a literal tree - and see
what you get. The `children` array is `readonly Tree<number>[]`, which is not an
empty tuple, so the recursion goes round for ever until the limit stops it. That
is the honest boundary of these types: they compute over *literal* tree shapes,
not over the general type. Say so in a comment.

## Hint 2

The runtime function is the counterweight to all of this. `collect` is one line
with `flatMap`, works on any tree of any depth, needs no type-level machinery,
and cannot fail. When you find yourself writing a type that duplicates what a
three-line function already does, ask what the type is buying.

## Hint 3

Four exports. The tree type is one line; `Leaves` and `Depth` are recursive
conditionals; `collect` is a `flatMap`.

Left to you: whether `collect` should be pre-order or post-order, and whether it
should be iterative. A deep tree will blow the JavaScript stack long before it
troubles the type checker.
